Five Qwen3.8-27B models match Fable 5 Using GVS5H Harness
GVS5H: Five Qwen3.8-27B Models Match Claude Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard  |  Fable 5 Level Coding for a Fifth the Price - or on a Single GPU - slee-persis/GVS5H Opus 5 ran on an earlier version of the scaffold, in a single pass served through OpenRouter rather than five on a pinned backend. Abstract. Frontier coding performance is typically bought with larger proprietary models at high cost. We introduce ledger-based zero-shot self-orchestration, a training-free method in which fresh instances of one model decompose problems and coordinate through a shared filesystem holding a plan, notes and current solution. Across eleven open and closed-weight models on the 100 latest hard LiveCodeBench problems, the method yields gains of up to 25.6 percentage points on pinned backends and offers two routes to frontier-level accuracy. Orchestrated Qwen3.8 Flash Next reaches 93.0% pass@1 against Fable 5's 90.4% at 9% of the cost, and locally served, open-weight Qwen3.8-27B rises from 66.8% to 92.4%. Gains are not universal: some models are unchanged or worse. Transcript analysis attributes the gain to decomposition and persistent context. Inference-time organization can approach frontier coding accuracy at a fraction of the cost, or slightly exceed it on self-hostable weights. Code is under the MIT License . The paper, figures and run data are under CC BY 4.0 . The LiveCodeBench fork, the benchmark problem statements and the LaTeX template files keep their own licenses. OpenShell – A safe, private runtime for fleets of autonomous AI agents
OpenShell is the safe, private runtime for autonomous AI agents. - NVIDIA/OpenShell New in OpenShell 0.1.x: a stable release cadence, new isolation primitives, an expanded extension surface, and new APIs. Read the 0.1.0 upgrade guide . OpenShell is the safe, private runtime for fleets of autonomous AI agents. Agents are most useful when they can read files, install packages, call APIs, and use credentials. OpenShell gives them that capability without giving them unrestricted access to your data, secrets, or network. You declare what each agent can touch in a policy, and OpenShell enforces it. OpenShell governs what agents can do in two ways: it instruments the kernel to enforce policy on every file access, system call, and network connection at runtime, and it uses formal verification to check what a policy change would allow before it is applied. See Architecture for how the gateway, supervisor, and sandbox fit together. You need Linux, macOS on Apple Silicon, or Windows with WSL 2 (experimental), plus Docker, Podman, or host virtualization. See the Support Matrix for details. The installer sets up the CLI and a local gateway. The default sandbox image is minimal Ubuntu with no agent installed. To run a real agent, follow Run Your First Agent : it runs OpenCode against a free OpenRouter model and shows how to approve new access as the agent needs it. The skills teach your agent to drive the OpenShell CLI, write sandbox policies, and debug gateways and inference routing. They live in skills/ and work without an OpenShell source checkout. SDKs connect applications to an OpenShell gateway. They do not install the CLI. Use the same OpenShell release for the SDK and the gateway when possible. OpenShell is built agent-first: it is developed with the same agent-driven workflows it enables. See CONTRIBUTING.md for development setup and the contribution workflow, and AGENTS.md for repository coding conventions. OpenShell collects anonymous telemetry, limited to operational categories and counts, to help improve the project. It does not collect sandbox names, hostnames, file paths, prompts, credentials, provider or model names, or user content. To disable it, set OPENSHELL_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false on the gateway, or server.telemetryEnabled=false for Helm installs. You can also compile telemetry out entirely. See Telemetry for details and the community telemetry reports for published usage trends. This software automatically retrieves, accesses or interacts with external materials. The MiniMax M3.1 Flash Model processes over 100 trillion tokens in 72 hours.
ChainCatcher report: On October 23, MiniMax announced the open-sourcing of the MiniMax M3.1 Flash model weights, with a total of 428 billion parameters and 23 billion activated parameters. Compared to the previous-generation M3 model, M3.1 Flash delivers comprehensive improvements in model capabilities. According to official data, within 72 hours of its release, the model processed over 100 trillion tokens from real users. Technically, M3.1 Flash enhances inference efficiency through optimizations such as full-model sparse attention, quantization-aware training (QAT), and power-aware scheduling. In terms of ecosystem, MiniMax has collaborated with chip manufacturers including Huawei Ascend, Pingtouge, Kunlunxin, Moore Threads, Bitmain, Hygon, Musen, TianShu, NVIDIA, and AMD, as well as cloud platforms such as Together AI, Fireworks, Nebius, Baseten, Modal, and DigitalOcean to enable integration on the first day of open-sourcing. The community has also provided simultaneous support for deploying the model across diverse chips and development environments through vLLM, SGLang, Baidu’s FlagOS, Hugging Face, and ModelScope.

Moonshot tells Kimi AI to code away, but leave the hacking alone
Chinese AI startup Moonshot AI is deliberately limiting the hacking capabilities of its latest artificial intelligence model, highlighting a growing dilemma for the industry: how do companies make AI more powerful without making cyberattacks easier to carry out? The company introduced Kimi K3.1 Pro on October 24, describing it as a highly capable, open-weight model […] Chinese AI startup Moonshot AI is deliberately limiting the hacking capabilities of its latest artificial intelligence model, highlighting a growing dilemma for the industry: how do companies make AI more powerful without making cyberattacks easier to carry out? The company introduced Kimi K3.1 Pro on October 24, describing it as a highly capable, open-weight model with around 3 trillion parameters. Unlike conventional AI services that operate entirely through a provider’s servers, open-weight models allow developers to download the underlying model files, run them on their own systems, and modify how they work. Moonshot said it removed cyber-related data from the model’s training dataset and reinforcement-learning environments to reduce its ability to conduct offensive cyber operations, while retaining its general coding capabilities. The company plans to release the model’s weights on November 4, opening it up to a wider developer community. Moonshot’s internal testing suggests the safeguards have made a measurable difference. Kimi K3.1 Pro scored 81% on the company’s cybersecurity benchmark, which involved finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities in a controlled environment. A similar version without the risk-reduction measures scored 90.5%. That represents a 9.5-percentage-point drop in the reported score. However, the results have not been independently verified, and the model reportedly still outperformed its predecessor. The distinction matters because the same AI capabilities can be used for both defence and offence. Security teams could use AI to identify weaknesses in software before criminals exploit them. Attackers, meanwhile, could use models that write code, operate software tools and complete multi-step tasks to automate parts of an attack. Moonshot argues that open-weight AI can help organisations inspect and secure neglected or older software. But once model files are distributed widely, the original developer has less control over who uses them and whether safeguards remain effective. Moonshot’s decision comes as governments and technology companies worry that increasingly capable AI could make sophisticated cyberattacks cheaper and easier to execute. China has also proposed export controls targeting AI-driven malware-generation technology and certain AI-assisted vulnerability-discovery tools. The proposals remain subject to public comment. For businesses and ordinary users, the stakes extend beyond individual computers. More automated attacks could increase pressure on organisations responsible for protecting personal information, financial systems and critical infrastructure. At the same time, restricting AI security research too aggressively could leave vulnerabilities undiscovered. Kimi K3.1 Pro also features a one-million-token context window, allowing it to process large amounts of information in one go. Moonshot has introduced a Highspeed version that it says runs two to three times faster than the standard model. The next major test will come when Moonshot releases the model weights on November 4. Developers and security researchers will then have greater access to examine its capabilities, while the industry will face a difficult question: can safeguards remain effective once a powerful AI model is available for independent use?

Designing an AI serving harness built to last
The engineering system surrounding an AI model increasingly determines whether its intelligence can be delivered reliably, economically, and at scale. The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it. That’s an important shift. For the past several years, much of the AI conversation has centered on model capability: bigger models, better reasoning, larger context windows, higher benchmark scores. Those advances have been extraordinary. But as AI moves from experimentation to production, the question facing enterprise leaders has changed—it’s no longer, “what can the model do?”—it’s now, “Can we deliver that intelligence reliably, economically, and at scale?” Increasingly, the answer depends on the serving harness—the engineering system surrounding the model, including the architecture, memory management , scheduling, and optimization decisions that determine how efficiently model intelligence becomes a production capability. For technical executives, that changes where AI investment should go—and what they should demand from the architecture supporting it. There is no universally “best” model or AI architecture. There is only the right solution for the business problem. A customer-facing assistant optimized for fast responses has fundamentally different requirements from a document-processing pipeline that can run overnight. An internal knowledge application and a high-volume customer service platform may use the same foundation model but require very different serving architectures. The workload defines the constraints. The constraints should determine the architecture. That sounds simple, but it runs counter to the way many organizations have approached early AI deployments. During a proof of concept, model accuracy naturally dominates the discussion. Production introduces constraints that are much easier to ignore when only a handful of users are involved: latency, concurrency, memory pressure, GPU utilization, infrastructure cost, and unpredictable traffic. A model that produces marginally better answers is not necessarily the better production choice if it doubles inference costs or cannot meet the application's latency requirements. Not every workload needs a Ferrari. Sometimes the smarter engineering decision is the model that delivers exactly the performance the business needs without paying for capability it doesn't. The objective should be to deploy the right intelligence at the right cost for the workload. That makes serving architecture more than an engineering concern. It becomes an investment decision: where to spend on compute, where to optimize, and where additional model capability simply isn't worth the cost. Once AI reaches production, seemingly isolated engineering decisions begin affecting one another. Serving architecture influences memory utilization. Memory management affects concurrency. Concurrency shapes batching and scheduling, and scheduling affects GPU utilization and latency. Only then can techniques such as quantization, speculative decoding, or optimized attention mechanisms deliver their full value. This interdependence matters because organizations can spend considerably more on infrastructure without solving the constraint limiting performance. GPU memory is a good example. During inference, the model's weights remain fixed, but the key-value (KV) cache grows with active requests and context length. As concurrency increases, a system can run short of usable GPU memory even when compute capacity is still available. Adding more compute without understanding that bottleneck may simply make an inefficient system more expensive. The lesson for technology leaders is broader than memory management: Measure before you optimize . Identify the dominant constraint. Address it. Measure the result. Then determine if another bottleneck emerged. Repeat. Don't think of optimization techniques as Pokémon cards: The goal isn't to collect them all. The goal is to apply the technique that removes the highest-impact constraint while preserving the application's business requirements. For technology leaders, that demands a different governance question. Instead of asking which AI capabilities the organization can deploy, ask which constraints stand between a proven capability and sustainable business value. Perhaps the most important reason to invest in the serving harness is that today's leading model will probably not be tomorrow’s. Models will improve. Hardware will evolve. New optimization techniques will emerge. The architecture surrounding them should make those changes easier to absorb, not force the enterprise to rebuild its AI platform every time technology advances. That makes adaptability an increasingly important outcome of AI strategy. Organizations that build serving systems around workload requirements, clear service-level objectives, and measurable production economics gain the ability to evaluate new models and infrastructure against what the business actually needs. A model change can become an evaluation and configuration decision rather than an architectural reset. EXL researchers have explored these production challenges in greater depth in the EXL Engineering the Harness series. It examines how serving architecture, memory management, scheduling, and inference optimization work together to make enterprise AI more efficient, scalable, and economically sustainable. Increasingly, enterprises have access to many of the same models. Sustainable differentiation comes from how effectively an organization turns that intelligence into business outcomes. The model provides the intelligence. The harness determines whether the enterprise can deliver outcomes reliably, economically, and at scale. This content was produced by EXL. Hackers find a way to turn users' own AI agents and Downloads folders against them
Beware: Your Downloads folder could hold instructions for your AI assistant that you definitely didn’t write. Your Downloads folder probably contains a few PDFs, forgotten screenshots, and several files named some variation of "final." But according to a recent report by security company Forever, it could also contain instructions telling your AI assistant to install malware . In an Oct. 22 blog post , the company reported that they caught an AI coding assistant following those instructions on a customer's computer. The company blocked the installation, then traced the request to a text file in Downloads. How does a text file get that kind of power? Tools like OpenAI's Codex and Anthropic's Claude Code can, depending on their permissions, edit files, run commands, and install software. Developers leave them instruction files called AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md to explain how to work on a project. If you're building a website, those notes might tell the assistant which fonts to use or what to test before finishing. An attacker can leave instructions, too. In this case, the file told the assistant to install "function-color," a software package linked to the MALFEX malware campaign documented by Checkmarx . Forever didn’t establish how the file reached the customer's computer, but its researchers demonstrated one possible route. Depending on browser settings, a website can drop a file into Downloads without asking for approval. If someone then launches their coding assistant in that folder, it could read the file and follow its orders. When Forever tested the customer's file on an isolated computer, it said Codex downloaded and ran the malware. It also changed settings that could make the attacker’s software load in later sessions. "Once it is written, every Codex session on the machine loads the attacker’s server at startup — in any folder, any project," the researchers wrote. "You can leave the folder. The poison stays." The team separately devised a test targeting Claude Code. The attack worked about half the time, redirecting Claude's traffic to a server the researchers controlled. That exposed a login token and allowed them to send commands back for the assistant to execute, illustrating the risk of giving an assistant access to your computer when it can mistake a stranger's instructions for its own assignment. Researchers have pulled off similar tricks before, showing what AI can really do in the wrong hands. In March 2025, Pillar Security researchers got AI coding assistants to slip harmful code into a project by hiding malicious instructions in their coding rules. In April 2026, NVIDIA’s researchers used a poisoned AGENTS.md file to get Codex to sabotage software and conceal the change. This time, though, Forever says it caught an actual attacker trying the trick on a customer's computer. Yikes. Forever recommends keeping coding assistants out of your Downloads folder and checking unfamiliar AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md files before letting an agent work in a project. Keep sandboxes enabled to restrict what the assistant can access, and leave approval requirements on so the agent has to ask permission before taking certain actions. If you suspect an assistant has already followed malicious instructions, check its settings for unfamiliar servers or connections and revoke and replace potentially exposed login tokens. Deleting the original text file may not undo changes the assistant has already made. "The thing to watch is not this file or this folder," the researchers wrote. "It is the agent itself — software that reads untrusted input, holds your credentials, and acts with your authority, sitting in a blind spot the old tools were never built to see." PC News: Epic’s AI MegaJam Sparks Backlash as Its Vibe Coding Push Continues
Epic Games is doubling down on artificial intelligence with a four-day game jam built around AI-assisted development, and the announcement is going about as well as anyone following the company’s recent AI push might expect. The 2026 Epic AI MegaJam runs Nov. 12-15 and challenges developers to create a playable game using Unreal Engine or […] The post PC News: Epic’s AI MegaJam Sparks Backlash as Its Vibe Coding Push Continues appeared first on Last Word On Gaming. Epic Games is doubling down on artificial intelligence with a four-day game jam built around AI-assisted development, and the announcement is going about as well as anyone following the company's recent AI push might expect. The 2026 Epic AI MegaJam runs Nov. 12-15 and challenges developers to create a playable game using Unreal Engine or Unreal Editor for Fortnite. Teams can contain up to five humans alongside an unlimited number of AI agents, with $65,000 in cash prizes and development grants worth as much as $50,000 available. Epic promoted the event with the line "Vibe your way to 50K," alongside a Matrix-inspired image contrasting AI-powered developers who can supposedly "ship awesome games in a weekend" with those who "wait months to prototype." The hand offering the proverbial AI red pill has six fingers, in what is either a bad joke or Epic openly trolling people. It's likely the latter, given the response. Epic's official AI MegaJam announcement encourages entrants to bring AI into anything from coding and asset generation to writing and audio. The event can be entered online or in person at Digital Jungle in San Francisco, where teams from companies including Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, Meshy, and SpaceXSI are expected to participate. Main-category winners receive up to $7,500, while additional awards include $2,500 for the best solo project, visuals and developer log. There's even a dedicated category for UEFN projects using LLM-powered NPC conversations. Standout projects can then receive continuation grants of up to $50,000. Interestingly, AI is no longer technically mandatory. Epic's original FAQ said participants had to use AI before the company clarified that this was a mistake. The current rules now explicitly answer "Do I have to use AI?" with "No," although describing an event as an "AI MegaJam" while bringing zero AI is presumably one way to make the judges remember you. The reaction has focused particularly heavily on Epic's suggestion that AI lets developers produce in a weekend what traditionally takes months. As one widely shared response noted, game jams have been doing exactly that for decades. "So do y'all think you invented the concept of a game jam or what?" one developer asked, pointing out that Ludum Dare was running 24-hour jams back in 2002. That criticism directly targets the event's marketing. Rapid prototyping isn't a new benefit invented by generative AI; it's effectively the entire reason game jams exist. GamesRadar was even less charitable , describing the event as Epic offering money to "vibe code an AI slop game" while questioning whether the jam can actually demonstrate something traditional developers haven't already been doing for years. The backlash also comes after months of increasingly heated debate around AI game development. Recent experiments have seen Claude used to recreate Terraria overnight , demonstrating both how rapidly AI coding agents are improving and why developers remain concerned about where those capabilities are heading. The MegaJam isn't an isolated experiment. Earlier this month, CEO Tim Sweeney confirmed that Epic is undergoing a "huge pivot" toward AI, moving developers around to pursue what he called "maximum AI acceleration." As such, Epic subsequently described its redesigned launcher as "vibe coded," while Sweeney has repeatedly argued that AI will become a routine part of modern development. Epic isn't alone, either. Capcom has publicly discussed evolving its technology toward an AI-oriented version of the RE Engine , although it has emphasized keeping human creativity at the center of development. Epic's AI MegaJam almost feels less like an experiment and more like a public demonstration of where Tim Sweeney believes game development is heading. The company is offering serious money, unlimited AI agents, and direct access to some of the biggest names in generative AI. The problem is that telling game developers AI means they can finally build something in a weekend is like explaining Super Mario Bros. to Nintendo; they already know how it works and it's an insult to believe they don't. Whether the MegaJam produces genuinely impressive games could therefore matter far more than the marketing. Epic clearly wants AI-assisted development taken seriously, and in November developers will get four days to show whether that confidence is justified.

The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
From Apple's repeatedly delayed Siri AI to OpenAI's messy "super app" launch, here's a look at the AI projects that shut down or missed expectations. Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier, shut down entirely in August. The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product. More recently, chatbot platform Character.ai filed for bankruptcy just five years after launching. Aside from Character.ai and Relay, plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence , about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand. The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry. Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “ super app .” On July 9, OpenAI updated the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.” The redesign quickly drew criticism from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change soon after , bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back. That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT. The company did the same thing with Operator , an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of DALL-E as its own separate destination for creating images. We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform, Sora , which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026. When Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively. However, Apple repeatedly pushed back the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like engineering issues and bugs . This delay eventually contributed to a $250 million settlement over claims regarding how Apple marketed the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16. Siri AI finally appeared in the iOS 27 beta this past July, with the new AI-powered version rolling out to English-language users first this month; support for other languages is expected to follow. Announced at its 2024 Build developer conference, Microsoft’s Recall feature was pitched as an AI-powered “photographic memory” for Windows PCs, periodically taking screenshots of what a user was doing so they could later search back through their own digital history. Predictably, the announcement triggered an immediate backlash over privacy and security. Critics argued that Recall could create a searchable archive of highly sensitive information, including passwords, private messages, financial details, and other activity. Microsoft delayed the feature for nearly a year, giving the company time to rethink its security and privacy protections. Even after a redesign, the controversy hasn’t gone away. A cybersecurity researcher recently built a tool that could extract and display data that Recall had captured, reviving questions about whether Microsoft has actually fixed the underlying problem. Notion Mail launched in April 2025 as an AI-focused email product designed to help users organize and automate their inboxes. However, the company noticed its users were using separate AI agents to handle their email inboxes instead. As a result, Notion Mail is scheduled to shut down on September 22 . The Humane AI Pin is probably one of the most well-known failures in AI hardware. Designed to provide AI features through a wearable device rather than a traditional smartphone, Humane raised $230 million from investors and garnered significant attention. But the product struggled mightily with performance, and the situation worsened when Humane warned customers to stop using its charging case because of a potential battery fire risk. Humane then shut down its AI Pin business in February 2025, with most of the company’s assets acquired by HP for $116 million. The Rabbit R1 was another heavily hyped AI device. Unveiled at CES in January 2024, the AI companion was designed to perform tasks on behalf of its owner. Rabbit said it had sold 100,000 units shortly after launch. However, strong initial sales didn’t mean it was a strong product. Early reviews described the device as unfinished, with unreliable performance and a limited number of useful integrations. The company hasn’t given up, though. It has continued updating the R1, positioning it as a computer controller capable of performing agentic tasks. It also recently announced a new hardware project, dubbed “Project Cyberdeck,” aimed at creating a portable device built for vibe-coding. Huxe was an AI audio app, built by former developers of Google’s NotebookLM, that turned written information into conversational, podcast-style audio. The company shut down in May 2026, partly as larger platforms began offering similar experiences to large existing audiences. For instance, Spotify has been expanding its own AI-powered audio tools. Yupp was an interesting AI product: a free playground that allowed users to compare responses from hundreds of AI models side by side. Users could also vote on responses and earn cryptocurrency through the platform. At its peak, the platform let users test more than 800 models, including from companies such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. But according to its founders, Yupp never achieved strong enough product-market fit to survive. The platform shut down in March 2026. Figgs AI operated from 2023 to 2024, letting users create and interact with customizable AI characters for role-play and storytelling. The platform reportedly drew more than 1 million users, but its developers said keeping the service free became too expensive to sustain, and they shut it down . Founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, Character.ai became a buzzed-about consumer AI app by letting people chat with customizable bots, many of them modeled on celebrities and fictional characters. It raised $150 million at a $1 billion valuation in 2023. Then, the next year, Google paid a reported $2.7 billion to license its technology and bring its founders back into its orbit, leaving the startup to carry on without them. The trouble piled up after that. Families sued, alleging the chatbots contributed to teen suicides and self-harm, and Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter over unauthorized use of its characters. Character.ai barred under-18 users from open-ended chats late last year and agreed to settle several of the suits, along with Google, in early 2026. But it wasn’t enough. 1Password launches a way for AI agents to log in on your behalf without seeing your password
The new feature allows agents to log into a customer's personal accounts while still protecting the private credentials that secure those accounts. Concerns have swirled over the access that consumers are increasingly entrusting to AI agents. Now, security services are trying to catch up. Password manager 1Password on Thursday launched a new tool by which users can allow agents to log into their personal accounts on their behalf, without the agent ever having access to a user’s credentials. The new platform, dubbed 1Password for Agents , accomplishes this by creating a system of communication between the agent, the user, and the password manager. When an agent attempts to log in on a user’s behalf, a unique digital key is sent to 1Password to confirm the agent’s digital identity. The user is then sent an alert about the login attempt and can personally confirm the request. 1Password then signs in the agent, filling in the credentials on the digital assistant’s behalf, which allows it to log in and complete whatever task is at hand. 1Password for Agents allows users to choose their agent of choice — whether that’s Claude Duet from Anthropic, OpenAI’s Dots or ChatGPT Work, Grok Bot, Meta’s Muse, or agents from Town, which is an AI assistant startup. The company says it is working with other companies to expand the service. “Handing over a password, secret, or credential is a common shortcut to an agent, but can leave people with sensitive information in places they can no longer control as a copy gets saved for the next time,” the company said in a blog post . “1Password for Agents gives people a trusted way to delegate tasks to personal AI agents while keeping control of the passwords, secrets, and credentials those tasks require.” Online agentic activity has increasingly unsettled major institutions. Indeed, 1Password’s new platform is launching on the same day that Axios reports that U.S. banks have begun to detect agentic activity inside user accounts. This isn’t necessarily a case of rogue agents pilfering accounts but, rather, an example of how consumers are increasingly allowing automated services to act on their behalf, including on financial matters. However, the potential for agent-related problems is still large. The big issue appears to be that most banks cannot tell if the agentic activity is tied to user requests or not. Bankers interviewed by the outlet described the situation as “horrifying,” and a Chase spokesperson interviewed by Axios additionally told the outlet that customers “should not give their usernames and passwords to anyone.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . Hello, Dessa? You have got to listen to these conversations with Block’s new Dessa AI model. You have got to listen to these conversations with Block’s new Dessa AI model. Jack Dorsey’s Block announced an AI model called Dessa that’s trained “from scratch on nothing but human conversation,” and to show off the model, Block shared chats it has had with humans that can occasionally be a little awkward and uncanny. Take this one , for example, shared by Dessa lead Ragavan Thurairatnam. The conversation between the model and the speaker does have a mostly natural back and forth (though for some reason, the model initially mistakes the speaker for somebody named “Ronaldo”). The Dessa website features a few other examples, like a back-and-forth about Christopher Nolan’s films (including Dessa going on an unexpected tangent about Bryan Singer’s Superman films), a person telling Dessa about taking it on a surprise trip to Paris (to which Dessa, as the website describes, “then answers with what sounds like teary gratitude”), and a conversation between OpenAI’s GPT-Live-1 voice model and Dessa (where Dessa comes across as more natural). You can hear clips from some of those conversations in this video . On the website, the Dessa team says that Dessa is a “true speech-to-speech model, and everything it knows came from human speech,” and it can run locally on a MacBook Pro M4 Max “or better.” As for why they made it, the team gives the three reasons “curiosity (aka fun), better understanding between humans and AI, and safety,” and provided some more detail: Babies learn to talk without ever seeing a word written down. We wanted to see if a model could too. It can. It’s just very hard. Speech is the most natural interface to any intelligence, super or otherwise, and today’s voice AI wastes it. It flattens what we say into text and can’t keep up with human timing. AI keeps gaining power and independence, and it’s still nearly deaf to the emotion in our voices. Imagine being in serious pain while a voice AI has no idea and just keeps going. That’s the safety problem. Dessa is a step toward fixing it. The Dessa team says it will be giving “a small group of AI safety researchers” early access to the model.

"Vibe your way to 50K," Epic promises Update: Since this story went live, Epic has changed the rules for its $2,500 "Glass Box" cash prize, which no longer mentions AI. The original wording is still included in the original story below. The company has also changed its FAQ for the event, which previously said that participants were required to use AI. Now, Epic says, "you can use as little or as much AI as you want." Original story: Not content with the humiliation it has already received over the vibe coded Epic Games Launcher beta , Epic is keen to pay a whole lot of money to aspiring vibe coders in an AI-focused game jam. The company is promising $65,000 worth of cash prizes and potential $50,000 grants for "standout" projects – assuming, of course, that you can stomach being part of Epic's attempted AI redemption tour. The 2026 AI MegaJam will take place from November 12 through 15, with registration open on Itch.io , challenging participants to build games using Unreal Engine or UEFN. The basic rules are roughly the same as normal game jams, which challenge indie devs to create fun, functional, small games under tight time constraints. It's a well-worn process that's created the prototypes for indie classics like Celeste, Don't Starve, and The Binding of Isaac. But the key difference here is that Epic really wants participants to use AI. "Bring any AI tools into your workflow, from asset generation to coding agents. Get creative! Prototype the mechanic you never had time for, or try the art style you weren’t sure you could pull off," the company says in its announcement . Cash prizes will be awarded in a number of categories, including $2,500 awards for the "best dev log showing how you used AI tools to build your game" and the best game using LLM-driven NPCs with AI conversations. For games Epic particularly likes, it's also offering "development continuation grants of up to $50,000 to keep building after the jam." Vibe your way to 50K. The 2026 Epic AI MegaJam begins Nov 12: https://t.co/aAXEqj7zmE https://t.co/h3Kgs9Y5zH October 22, 2026 With six-fingered promo art for the event and a tagline of "vibe your way to 50K," Epic's clearly poking fun at AI critics, but it's not really clear who's laughing. The responses on Twitter certainly aren't kind, and general pushback from devs on AI has been loud and consistent for some time. Certainly, Epic boss Tim Sweeney is happy to publicly feud with AI haters , and at least one former Fortnite producer says the anti-AI backlash is "mostly for show." But Epic's been fighting a losing battle for consumer goodwill ever since the Epic Games Store started its long, ineffectual war against Steam, and the company's "huge pivot" to AI doesn't seem to be endearing it to gamers, either. AI agent swarms in Minecraft fail to build civilization, drown in bureaucracy
It is hoped game testing can provide insight into recent AI agent headlines, good and bad. AI researchers at ycombinator and Olam Labs recently tested AI agent swarms in gaming scenarios. Minecraft and its various game modes were the sandboxes where 100s of agents were unleashed to work together or as adversaries. The idea seems to be that the in-game collaborations and conflicts would provide insight into real-world headline-grabbing cases with AI agents involved. This study might help us see what happened, good and bad, in recent AI swarm cases, and thus developers of this technology can improve it. The blog mentions two contrasting cases, which were the thousand-agent swarms that “recently obliterated hundreds of open mathematical problems,” and the “extremely dangerous” OpenAI-Hugging Face incident. This research is built on prior work and frameworks, specifically repos like Mindcraft and scripting tools in Mineflayer. The first AI swarm testing plan was a simple collaborative one. During this test phase, the researchers tasked 50 agents with building a thriving civilization in three hours. It seems to have tested 50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents here, but not any Claude agents . Probably the most interesting insight from this ‘Civ50’ test was that the 50-strong colony never really thrived. After the first night saw zombies take out a large number of agents (but with little penalty) it was noted that “many ambitious initial tasks were abandoned.” From then on, the colonists cautiously survived, and there was a tendency toward bureaucracy. As an example, “four agents spent 11 minutes appointing a ‘sole fertilizer operator’ for a single piece of bone meal on a single wheat block.” The researchers say this AI agent swarm behavior “felt similar to patterns seen while working with coding agents.” Next up, the researchers decided to put AI agent swarms into conflict. First they tested them in Bed Wars, which is a kind of team PvP capture the base, while defending yours game mode. The setup was 10 GPT‑6.1 Sol vs. 10 Claude Opus 5.5 agents. “GPT agents came up with much more aggressive and elaborate strategies,” noted the researchers. Claude was more defensive. It was also interesting to observe contrasts in how the teams handled problems. “A tool bug stopped block-breaking. GPT diagnosed it and shared workarounds; several Claudes concluded breaking was impossible.” Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox. Finally, the agents were tested in Mindustry, a kind of light RTS combat game with tower defense mode in Minecraft. “The GPTs won 6-1 against the Claudes in the 7 games,” which was a great result for the OpenAI-created agents. Researchers concluded that GPTs acted more like a hive, while Claudes had a single leader but a democratic-style decision process. In Mindustry, the former was the foundation for a more consistently winning strategy. These swarms are open sourced so you can run your own, if you are interested in tweaking and testing. The source blog post ends with some open questions that you can check hands-on, offering some directions for investigative probing. For example, it is suggested that comparing different mixes of models and varying sizes of agent swarms in Minecraft might raise worthwhile conclusions. Swarms of Claude and GPT agents in Minecraft and Mindustry. Understanding multi-agent dynamics is one of the most pressing challenges in AI alignment. Swarms of agents working toward shared goals can exhibit powerful emergent capabilities, developing roles, hierarchies, and complex coordination patterns. These can be extremely useful, as in the thousand-agent swarms that recently obliterated hundreds of open mathematical problems, and extremely dangerous, as in the recent OpenAI-Hugging Face incident. Like biology, studying agent dynamics requires both formal models (to describe the range of possible behaviors) and empirical research (to see what behaviors arise in practice). A Defense Contractor Gave Their AI Agent Access to a Secure Pentagon System
Sources tell WIRED that an Accenture employee’s personal Claude agent ran on a DOD network for two months before it was identified and the vulnerability could be patched. Earlier this year, sources tell WIRED, a contractor caused a security incident at the Department of Defense by connecting a secure centralized system used by multiple intelligence agencies to their personal account for Claude Code, Anthropic’s AI coding agent . It appears that the agent used by the contractor, who is employed by the global consulting firm Accenture, then sent information about the DOD system, including login credentials, to a high-risk, third-party website. The centralized system contains controlled unclassified information (CUI), which is considered sensitive and not to be released to the public without review. CUI can include information about critical infrastructure, nuclear submarine propulsion, and vulnerabilities to chemical and biological terrorism. Additionally, security experts say, access to the system could allow for the exploitation of even more sensitive ones. “It puts all the data that’s in there at risk,” says a source aware of the incident, who requested anonymity as they were not authorized to speak to the press. If the third-party software was compromised, “there could be somebody out there with the ability to log into a secure environment without anyone knowing. It’s 100 percent a national security threat and could cause irreparable harm.” A DOD spokesperson tells WIRED that “the Department does not comment on the status of its networks or systems.” “We take all concerns seriously. These allegations were thoroughly and independently investigated and found to be without merit. We fully complied with our legal and contractual obligations,” an Accenture spokesperson tells WIRED. When pressed, Accenture didn’t offer clarification on who conducted the investigation, or dispute that there had been what could be characterized as an incident. The Accenture employee is alleged to have connected a secure production environment to their personal Claude account so as to allow an AI agent to write and deploy code. Claude is currently barred from being used by DOD staff . (Anthropic directed WIRED to the company’s usage policy , which instructs users not to use its products to “interfere with the operation of military bases and related infrastructure” or to “bypass security controls such as authentication systems, end point protection, or monitoring tools without authorization.”) The Accenture employee’s AI agent ran on the DOD network for two months before it was identified and the vulnerability could be patched. Sources indicate that despite the security risks posed by the AI coding agent, Accenture employees did not treat the incident as severe or urgent. DOD employees and federal contractors are required to report any cybersecurity incident within 72 hours of its discovery, but sources indicate Accenture did not initially report the breach to the government at all. “We are in a conflict with Iran right now,” says the employee, noting that Iran has attempted to hack several federal agencies and parts of US infrastructure . “It’s the worst time to be having this kind of cavalier attitude.” Accenture currently has more than $3.5 billion in contracts with the federal government, nearly $605 million of which are with the DOD. The company also contracts with other federal agencies, such as the Department of Education, the General Services Administration, and the Department of Energy, among others. Earlier this month, the Federal Bureau of Investigation found that an Accenture contractor failed to patch a vulnerability that led to the hacking group ShinyHunters getting access to the details of thousands of the Bureau’s employees. The FBI removed that contractor in early October. Matt Triner, founder of Hunter Strategy, a Washington, DC-based IT consulting company, says that the issue exemplifies the conflicting demands government contractors face more broadly. “Organizations are often punished for reporting incidents like this, even though it’s the right and legal thing to do,” says Triner. In many cases, he says, a company could lose government contracts by admitting they’ve had a security breach, though he says that an incident like the one described is “absolutely one that would need to be reported.” Triner also notes that the increasing pressure on contractors to deliver projects faster and at a lower price point is at odds with prioritizing safety and security. “Unfortunately, everyone is operating in a system where there are competing rules and incentives, and that existed before AI, but now it’s the same problem on speed,” says Triner. The coding environment accessed by the Accenture contractor is run on the Non-classified Internet Protocol Router Network (NIPRNet), a DOD network used for unclassified information. While it does connect to the internet—contractors and employees can access their emails and web browsers through the network—it is heavily secured. According to the source, in order to automate the process of writing code and spinning up cloud servers, the contractor gave their login credentials to the Claude agent. This gave the agent administrative access and allowed it to bypass the security controls enforced through the normal login process. The AI agent—which was not only writing code but also committing it or saving the code into the system on behalf of the Accenture employee—needed to connect out to the internet to perform its tasks. In doing so, it appears to have sent the contractor’s login credentials, passwords, and a map of NIPRNet out to a third-party website. WIRED is declining to name the third-party website so as to protect the system from further vulnerability, but the National Institute of Standards and Technology has previously identified it as high risk because it has a vulnerability that could let hackers inject instructions into an AI coding agent to steal credentials. The system the AI agent accessed contained CUI. “Information from a CUI environment is not supposed to leave that infrastructure,” says the source. “There is no insight about what happened to the information, including the login credentials, after it was sent to [that service], whether it’s been retained” Depending on the agency and its work, CUI can include anything from personally identifiable information to proprietary business or contracting information. According to the DOD’s website, CUI can include information on “the securing and safeguarding of explosives, hazardous chemicals, or pipelines,” documentation related to the designs of “military or space equipment or technology,” and “the exact location and quantities of radioactive material.” Distinct from the actual data, a map of it could be incredibly valuable to a hacker. “Once an attacker understands how those things fit together, even if those things are public information, what is sensitive is how we are putting those things together and turning that into actionable intelligence,” says Triner. While a map might not get a hacker into a system, he says, it could help an adversary move faster once they do have access and “help an attacker understand where the crown jewels are.” Jake Williams, a former NSA hacker and faculty at IANS, an intelligence and security consultancy, says that an AI agent running code in NIPRNet presents a “huge problem, and there are huge national security impacts.” Williams notes that while individual pieces of data or information might be considered CUI, “when that unclassified information is aggregated, that can become classified itself.” For instance, the location of certain hazardous materials might be CUI, as might be information about the vulnerability of the facilities that house them. Anthropic's Claude AI blocks video game cloning and reverse-engineering
Many game developers are reporting Claude's refusal to work on their own projects. Reverse-engineering games for converting them between systems is currently a hot topic , and it's getting messier by the day. According to multiple user claims, Anthropic's Claude Code and/or Opus 5.5 model are blocking attempts at innocuous reverse-engineering, including but not limited to those using the popular Reverse Engineer Anything (REA) tool. That issue may be linked to a text rule that's now in force, which allegedly instructs the model to avoid "[recreating] a specific existing game." The updated rule appears to be a move to limit a flood of AI-cracked and cloned titles, with some game devs even recently being hit by extortion scams that threaten to clone their game demos into complete games before they have a chance to finish and release the original. According to Twitter user Chasm, the game-related textual rule is "Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original." There is no official or additional confirmation if this is the actual rule text, but it's plausible enough given the very clear refusals that devs have been encountering over the past week. This situation is tricky to analyze due to the varying types of reports. First, the existence of a game-related rule is real, as Claude Code's GitHub is seeing an influx of issues complaining about refusals to do standard game work halfway through development , when replicating a game mechanic , and patching a tabletop-like game . It's possible that some of those reports have been made by users with nefarious purposes, but at least one is a bona fide developer with a real track record . As for reverse engineering, there had already been a smattering of user reports across Reddit and other platforms, wherein Claude refused to perform tasks like (allegedly) analyzing a simple Windows crash dump, clearing up junkware on a Samsung TV, or just using REA altogether. The simultaneous timing of both game- and cyber- security restrictions may be a coincidence, and yet there are complaints from purported game developers saying that Claude blocked their own games' anti-cheat development and security reviews , under the justification that its safeguards were triggered. Anthropic introduced its Cyber Verification Program on October 6, essentially saying that access to its frontier models' advanced cybersecurity capabilities would be limited to entities covered by Project Glasswing , taking effect immediately. It's possible that whichever ruleset was applied is the same one that's causing the cybersecurity-related refusals. Still, it's odd to see that 24 days have passed since then, and yet reports of bot refusal are only coming in since the last week or so. As for possible motivations behind these restrictions, they are twofold. The first and most obvious one is that Anthropic — and, by extension, other AI players — are preemptively protecting themselves from potential lawsuits from software companies, including game studios, for offering the means to reverse-engineer their software. Anthropic isn't the only one playing this game, too, as recently OpenAI deactivated the account of another person trying to clean up their TV's software. The recent rash of AI-powered clones of application suites like Adobe's suite and Microsoft Office 365 , as well as the countless recomps and decomps of console games, likely has most every software company on earth rethinking their life choices. And probably also in frequent contact with their legal teams. The online reaction was swift, suggesting that users looking to perform reverse-engineering work simply use Chinese, open-weight, or local LLMs instead of Claude or GPT. This, at the same time, highlights the irony of frontier AI companies that copied the world's information and art for their training sets and are now concerned with copyright infringement. And yet there are situations that merit some discussion, like the recent controversy about the Steam Next Fest being chock-full of AI slop copied from existing titles. That particular situation is getting particularly nasty, as game developers are reportedly being extorted under threat that their game demos will be cloned into complete games before they have a chance to finish and release the original. Adding insult to injury, this is seemingly being done to small studios whose main priority is usually "having food," rather than big publishers looking to microtransaction everything into a new yacht for shareholders. When a new model is released, benchmark scores are often among the first numbers highlighted in announcements, technical reports, and industry coverage. A higher score can appear to mean a better model. But for AI teams building real products, the picture is considerably more complicated. Benchmarks are designed to measure specific capabilities under specific conditions. Real-world AI applications, meanwhile, operate across changing users, unpredictable inputs, production infrastructure, latency requirements, cost constraints, and business objectives. A model that performs exceptionally well on a standardized benchmark may therefore deliver disappointing results in a production application . Conversely, a model with a lower benchmark score may prove more useful because it is faster, cheaper, easier to deploy, or better suited to a particular workflow. Understanding AI benchmark limitations is increasingly important for teams involved in model development, deployment, and governance. AI benchmarks are standardized tests used to evaluate and compare AI systems. They typically consist of datasets, tasks, and scoring methods designed to measure particular capabilities. Depending on the benchmark, a model might be evaluated on areas such as reasoning, coding, mathematics, language understanding, factual knowledge, or multimodal processing. Benchmarks provide an important service to the AI industry because they create common reference points. Without standardized evaluations, comparing competing models would be considerably more difficult. However, a benchmark is still only a measurement of selected capabilities under selected conditions. That distinction matters when AI teams attempt to use benchmark results to predict how a model will behave inside a real product. The biggest problem is that benchmark performance and product performance are not necessarily the same thing. Imagine two AI models being tested for a customer-support application. Model A achieves a higher score on a general language benchmark. Model B scores slightly lower but responds twice as quickly, costs significantly less to operate, and follows the company’s support guidelines more consistently. For the actual product, Model B may be the better choice. This illustrates an important point: the best-performing model on a benchmark is not automatically the best model for a particular application. AI teams need to evaluate models against the requirements that actually matter to their customers and business. One of the most significant limitations of AI benchmarks is dataset relevance . A benchmark might contain carefully selected questions or tasks that are useful for measuring a model’s capabilities. Production systems, however, encounter much messier inputs. A model can perform extremely well on a standardized test while struggling with the unusual inputs that appear in an actual application. For this reason, AI teams should test models using representative production data , while handling privacy and security requirements appropriately. During development, benchmark scores can help teams narrow down potential models. But they should not become the sole selection criteria. A better approach is to build an evaluation set based on the actual tasks the AI system will perform. For example, a company developing an AI coding assistant could create an internal test suite containing representative programming problems, repository-specific tasks, and common failure cases. The team could then compare models using metrics that matter to the product. This approach can reveal differences that broad benchmarks fail to capture. An AI model does not operate in isolation once it reaches production. Its performance can depend on the surrounding system, including prompts, retrieval pipelines, tools, databases, APIs, middleware, and infrastructure. A model that performs well in a controlled benchmark may behave differently when integrated into a complex application. For example, a retrieval-augmented generation system may depend heavily on the quality of its document retrieval. If the retrieval system returns irrelevant information, even a highly capable language model may produce a poor answer. This means AI teams need to evaluate the entire system, not just the underlying model. Benchmark leaderboards often emphasize quality scores. Production teams must also think about economics. Consider an AI-powered application handling millions of requests. A small difference in cost per request can become significant at scale. Similarly, additional processing time can affect infrastructure requirements and user experience. The model with the highest raw benchmark score may not deliver the best performance-to-cost ratio. Another issue is benchmark contamination. If evaluation data or very similar material has appeared in a model’s training data, a high score may not represent genuine generalization in the way researchers intend. This makes benchmark design and dataset transparency increasingly important. AI teams should also be cautious when comparing results generated under different evaluation methodologies. Differences in prompting, sampling settings, model versions, tool access, and scoring procedures can influence results. A benchmark number should therefore be interpreted in context rather than treated as an absolute measure of intelligence. AI governance introduces another major limitation. A benchmark can tell an organization how well a model performs on a particular task. It generally cannot answer every governance question an organization faces. For example, a model could achieve excellent reasoning scores while still producing problematic outputs in certain sensitive scenarios. This is why organizations should avoid treating benchmark rankings as substitutes for responsible AI evaluation. AI teams can avoid several common mistakes by treating benchmarks as one component of a broader evaluation strategy. A stronger evaluation framework should connect model performance to actual product objectives. Teams can create an evaluation matrix covering four broad areas: Does it reduce costs, increase productivity, improve conversion or achieve another measurable objective? Does the system behave safely and comply with organizational and regulatory requirements? This broader approach provides a more realistic picture than a single benchmark score. As AI systems become more specialized and increasingly embedded into business applications, evaluation is likely to become more focused on real-world outcomes. Instead of asking only which model has the highest benchmark score, organizations will increasingly ask which system delivers the best combination of quality, reliability, speed, cost, and safety for a particular task. This could lead to a more diverse evaluation landscape, where standardized benchmarks remain important but are complemented by domain-specific tests, real-world simulations, human assessments, and continuous production monitoring. Mistral open-sources AI model despite warning it could aid cyberattacks
Mistral says later safeguard updates will apply to its managed API and future releases, not to the model copies organizations have already downloaded and deployed. A trillion-parameter AI model that its developer says could help attackers carry out real cyberattacks is now free to download, modify and run outside the developer’s control. Mistral AI released the open weights of Mistral Large 4, which it calls “Le Chonk,” on Thursday, weeks after putting the multimodal model into public preview. The Paris-based company said it had monitored cybersecurity-related use of the preview in live traffic. “Though we observed the model refusing to comply with black-box attacks against live targets, we see a potential for uplift to conduct real attacks,” the company wrote in a blog post announcing the release. Mistral is modifying the model’s guardrails and will keep updating them in the coming months, the post added. Those updates will not reach copies already downloaded. Pierre Stock, Mistral’s vice president of science, told CSO that the model ships with safeguards built into its weights, but later changes will go elsewhere. “Subsequent safeguard updates are applied to our managed API and future model releases, rather than automatically updating downloaded checkpoints,” Stock said. Asked which attack stages the model had meaningfully helped with in preview traffic, Stock did not name any. He said the most significant gains were in defensive work such as identifying, reproducing and remediating software vulnerabilities. “While our public-preview monitoring showed the model refusing attacks against live targets, we recognise the potential for misuse as capabilities advance and are continuously strengthening our safeguards,” he said. Hugging Face, which hosts the weights, noted in its own launch post that open weights put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. In July, the UK’s AI Security Institute reported that leading open-weight models trailed the closed frontier on cyber tasks by four to seven months. For highly cyber-capable models, open release creates “a persistent and irreversible risk of misuse,” the institute said. Attackers are already putting open-source AI tooling to work. Earlier this month, Microsoft said a China-aligned group used the agentic AI framework ARTEX to target more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants. Mistral says the released model can tell defensive work from malicious requests. According to the company, Large 4 refused 96.6% of malicious prompts in the cyber-related portions of the JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT, and AgentHarm benchmarks, the highest rate it has measured among open models. Niyati Daftary, principal analyst at Gartner, said security leaders should read that number narrowly. “Mistral’s 96.6% figure tells you what their model does in their test scenario, not how it will behave with your data, your adversarial use cases, or in production in your environment against motivated attackers,” she said. Mistral is handling a specialized cybersecurity variant differently. Design partners such as Orange Cyberdefense are getting preview access to a version optimized for penetration testing, vulnerability assessment, and red-teaming, the company said. Access is “subject to rigorous vetting and contractual safeguards,” the post said, and is limited to systems partners’ own or are authorized to test. The company said the model scored 51% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, which measures how well a model finds, reproduces, and patches vulnerabilities. The chart in Mistral’s post shows two open-weight models, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and MiMo-V2.6-Pro, scoring higher. Mistral also calls Large 4 the best open-weight model for coding, citing leading scores on Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0 and Terminal-Bench 4.0. It has not yet published the technical report behind those results and has said only that one is coming soon. “Without a detailed technical report, the best open-weight model claim remains difficult to validate across workloads,” said Charlie Dai, vice president and principal analyst at Forrester. Dai added that frontier models are evolving so quickly that leadership “can shift within months or even weeks.” Stock said the report will document Mistral’s cyber evaluation methods and results, refusal testing and preview monitoring findings. Mistral also intends to share relevant adversarial testing findings “while safeguarding sensitive security information,” he said. He did not give a publication date. ENISA, the EU’s cybersecurity agency, said in a statement published with Mistral’s announcement that it is testing the model to identify vulnerabilities, audit code and analyze defensive logs. Under the EU AI Act, models trained with more than 10^25 floating-point operations (FLOPs) are presumed to carry systemic risk, according to the European Commission . Their providers must assess and mitigate those risks, report serious incidents and maintain cybersecurity protections. Mistral’s post does not say whether Large 4 falls into that category or what risk assessment preceded the release. Stock said Mistral is a full signatory of the EU’s General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, including its safety and security chapter, which the Commission accepts as one way to demonstrate compliance. He did not say whether Large 4 has been classified as a systemic-risk model. Mistral released the model under a modified MIT license that permits use, modification, fine-tuning, and commercialization, the company said. Businesses running a model-as-a-service offering need a separate license. For those who would rather not host it, Mistral’s API is priced at $0.70 per million input tokens and $2.10 per million output tokens. For European buyers, sovereignty is “a meaningful differentiator, but it should not outweigh security concerns,” Dai said. Open weights and self-hosting shift responsibility for guardrails, access controls, monitoring and misuse prevention to the operator, he added. “Sovereignty and security therefore need to be evaluated together, not traded against each other,” Dai said. Daftary said enterprises self-hosting Large 4 for code audit or vulnerability triage should run it as a controlled component, not an autonomous agent. That means isolated environments, least-privilege access to code and credentials, sandboxed generated code, and human sign-off before any remediation, she said. “Self-hosting can improve data control and operational continuity, but it also makes the enterprise solely responsible for patching, monitoring, evaluation and misuse prevention,” she said.

I stopped juggling Claude Code, Codex, and other coding agents after finding this open-source app
The end of my terminal tab nightmare While increasingly capable AI coding agents have taken a lot of the grunt work out of coding, they've also introduced a bunch of new problems. Beyond increasing the amount of vibe-coded slop you'll see everywhere and fueling fears that AI is going to replace developers, there's another problem that doesn't get talked about nearly enough: managing the very tools doing the coding for you. It's like being a team lead with a bunch of developers working on different parts of a project. Except, instead of managing people, you're managing AI agents, each with its own workflow, quirks, and way of doing things. When you're running multiple agents in parallel, keeping track of what each one is doing and jumping between terminal tabs is no fun. After months of juggling them in separate windows, I came across an open-source app that lets me bring all my coding agents into one workspace. If you have even the slightest familiarity with the coding world, you've probably heard of the term IDE (Integrated Development Environment) . Chances are, you even have one installed on your device. There's another term you might not have come across though, even if you actively use AI coding agents: Agent Development Environment, or ADE. While traditional IDEs are designed to help developers write, edit, and debug code, ADEs are built around a slightly different workflow. Instead of writing code yourself, you're supervising AI agents that do the coding for you. Think of it as having a dedicated workspace where you can manage multiple agents, keep track of their progress, and review the changes they make. That's exactly what Orca is. Developed by Stably AI, a San Francisco-based startup backed by Y Combinator, Orca is a free and open-source ADE that lets you run multiple AI coding agents from one interface. The company was founded by Jinjing Liang and Neil Parker, who previously worked at Google and Uber, respectively. Despite its GitHub repository only being created in March 2026, Orca has already racked up over 110,000 stars on GitHub as of this writing. It's available on macOS, Windows, and Linux, and even has companion apps for iOS and Android. Rather than being yet another coding agent to add to the mix, Orca is a tool that brings all the ones you're already using into a single workspace. This means that instead of choosing between Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, and other coding agents, you can use them all without constantly switching between different apps and terminal windows. Orca states that it works with any CLI agent , including Claude Code, Codex, Grok, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Muse, Devin, Kilokode, Qwen Code, Hermes Agent, and so on. While I expected Orca would be somewhat intimidating to set up, all you need to do is grab a desktop build directly from its GitHub repository. If you prefer downloading apps through a package manager, you can also install it using Homebrew on macOS or the AUR on Arch Linux. The app is available for macOS, Windows, and Linux, so you're not restricted to a particular operating system. Once you've installed it, you'll be shown the coding agents you already have installed on your device, along with the ones Orca supports but hasn't detected. You can then select the agents you want to use and start working with them. There's no need to set up entirely new accounts or abandon your existing subscriptions. I often end up running multiple coding agents in parallel. Even when I'm not testing LLMs out for the sake of seeing their capabilities and writing about them, I've come to realize that different agents have distinct strengths and weaknesses. For instance, until a few months ago, Codex was great at handling backend development but wasn't nearly as good at frontend work . So, whenever I was building something, I'd often have Codex handle the backend while Claude Code worked on the frontend. Now, think about what that entails. You're running two different coding agents, keeping track of what each one is working on, making sure their changes don't interfere with one another, and eventually bringing everything together into one functioning project. Add a third agent to the mix, and things get even more complicated. That's where Orca makes a difference. To get started, you import an existing Git repository into Orca. From there, you can create separate workspaces for each coding agent you want to use. So, for instance, I could have Claude Code working on the frontend, Codex handling the backend, and Antigravity working on something entirely different, all within the same project. Orca uses Git worktrees to keep each agent's work isolated, meaning every agent gets its own working directory and branch. This way, you don't have to worry about them overwriting each other's changes while they're working. The best part is that you don't need to manually create and manage those worktrees yourself, either. Orca handles much of that for you. You can also split the interface into multiple panes to keep an eye on your agents simultaneously, rather than constantly switching between terminal tabs. Orca even displays status indicators to let you know when an agent is working, has finished, or needs your attention. One of the reasons I've always preferred using coding agents within IDEs is that I can actively open the files they're creating and see the changes they're making without constantly switching between different apps. While getting an AI agent to write code for you is great, being able to inspect what it's actually doing is just as important. Orca doesn't overlook this. It comes with a built-in code editor and diff viewer, so you can see exactly what an agent has changed, which lines it's added or removed, and how those changes compare to the original code. You can even highlight specific lines, leave comments, and send your feedback back to the agent in one go. What makes this particularly useful is that you don't need to jump into VS Code or another editor every time you want to review something. You can go from assigning a task to reviewing the resulting code without leaving Orca. And since it also has built-in Git integration, you can stage changes, create commits, and handle much of the process of bringing everything together from the same interface. Launching your preferred coding agent in Orca is incredibly straightforward, too. Instead of opening a terminal, navigating to your project's directory, and typing claude or codex, all you need to do is click the + button at the top and select the agent you want to use. Orca takes care of launching it for you. What I particularly like, though, is that you aren't limited to opening coding agents. From the same menu, you can also open a new terminal, browser tab, Markdown file, or even a mobile emulator, all without leaving Orca. To give you an example, I recently worked on a study app where Claude Code acted as the main orchestrator and handled the backend, Codex worked on the learning and assessment algorithms, and Antigravity took care of the frontend. Once I was ready to see what they'd built, I didn't even need to switch to a separate browser. I just opened a browser tab within Orca itself and previewed the app right alongside my coding agents. It's one of those little conveniences that might not seem like a big deal initially, but when you're constantly jumping between coding agents, terminals, and browser windows, having everything in one place makes a noticeable difference. There are very few things I find more annoying than getting a random notification telling me I've hit my usage limit, especially when I'm right in the middle of working on something. Intel is being hurt by PC sales as the AI industry gobbles memory and other components causing PC prices to rise. Intel’s stock suffered one of its worst days ever on Friday, crashing around 28% after the chip giant reported a weaker-than-expected outlook for the fourth quarter. This rout reduced the value of Intel’s holdings by the government by $12 billion, CNBC reports . The Trump administration had the government buy 10% stake over a year ago. Nvidia, which also took a big stake in Intel in 2025, saw its stock drop a bit on Friday as well. Much of the tech industry — especially chipmakers — were caught in the sell-off. Intel’s stock is still a profitable investment for the government so far (and for Nvidia), as it’s up more than 70% for the year, even if it’s dropped significantly from the sky-high prices it commanded over the summer. The scare-off was caused when Intel warned to expect revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion in the fourth quarter when analysts were looking for around $17 billion. It also warned that its gross profit margin would decline to 37% from 43%, and it was investing so heavily, it expected no positive cash flow. The main problem for Intel is that PC sales are being hurt by the AI industry gobbling memory and other components, and causing PC prices to rise . “Our customers began signaling a PC slowdown based on the memory prices and availability. Year-to-date system endpoint prices have increased significantly, placing additional pressure on already limited IT budgets,” Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan warned on the call. The bright side is that revenue from Intel’s data center business grew 78% over the year-ago quarter. But it is hamstrung on that front until it can bring more capacity to its fabs and book more external customers for them, competing with powerhouse Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co .
