America’s AI Chip War Is Heating Up in the Dumbest Possible Ways
The Trump administration announced plans to clamp down on China’s access to AI chips. Apparently, the cheating scandal of the century was the motivation they were missing. This week, the Trump administration made it significantly harder for Chinese companies to access some of the world’s most advanced AI chips. For years, tech firms like Alibaba and ByteDance could rent computing power from data centers overseas, allowing them to use powerful Nvidia chips they were generally prohibited from physically importing into China . This is known as remote access. But under new plans announced on Monday, overseas data centers that want to provide large amounts of computing power to China will have to get special licenses and deal with other annoying new kinds of red tape. The White House also imposed stricter rules on shipments of advanced chips to five countries, including Singapore and Malaysia, where US officials suspect significant levels of smuggling may have taken place. These are not new policy ideas, and similar proposals have been kicking around in Washington for a while. But the timing of Monday’s announcement is impossible to ignore. Yes, this is about Jensen Huang’s sex life. As you’ve probably heard by now, the Nvidia cofounder resigned as CEO last week after admitting he had an affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman accused of having ties to Chinese intelligence services. Alice previously worked at the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which offered remote access services and is suspected of engaging in chip smuggling. The scandal may have been so embarrassing for the White House that officials felt compelled to demonstrate they had the situation under control. Apparently, the cheating scandal of the century was the motivation they were missing. (A White House spokesperson previously told WIRED that the new rule would “crack down on the smuggling of advanced US SI chips” and “help ensure that America’s most advanced chips go first to US SI innovators, not Chinese shell companies.”) It started in the fall of 2022, when the Biden administration unveiled a set of rules that would radically alter the future of AI and who was allowed to build it. The goal was to choke off China's access to the advanced chips needed to train the world's most powerful AI models, as well as the equipment required to manufacture those chips. It's worth remembering just how radical this approach was at the time. For decades, the US had used export controls to keep sensitive American technology away from specific military programs, governments, and blacklisted companies accused of carrying out human rights abuses. But the Biden administration was attempting something far more ambitious: using Washington's influence over the global semiconductor industry to hold back the world's second-largest economy from competing at the cutting edge of one of the most important new technologies in generations. The strategy rested on a relatively simple idea. Training the most advanced AI models requires enormous amounts of computing power, and American companies like Nvidia dominate the market for the chips that provide it. By restricting China's access to those chips, Washington hoped to preserve America's technological lead. Four years later, the US certainly cannot claim total victory. But boy, have things gotten messy. Part of the problem is that Washington tasked the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), a relatively small, underfunded agency within the Commerce Department, with leading enforcement of the controls. The bureau had a budget of just $235 million in 2026—a paltry sum compared to what Nvidia rakes in in a single week. The bureau's job only got harder as the Biden administration introduced successive rounds of increasingly complex restrictions, scrambling to tighten the rules as chipmakers found increasingly elaborate ways to get around them. But one of the bureau's biggest challenges was fighting what became a booming industry for smuggling AI chips into China. At BIS, Megaspeed has become a poster child for the problem, although it's far from the only company suspected of involvement, or even the largest, according to a person familiar with the matter. According to Bloomberg, roughly 50,000 of the estimated 136,000 AI chips Megaspeed imported into Malaysia and Indonesia in 2024 and 2025 weren't accounted for in Nvidia's initial inventory checks. It's not clear where they may have ended up. (Nvidia later said it had found at least some of them.) Even if all of the unaccounted-for chips ended up in China, they would represent only a fraction of the advanced semiconductors believed to have been smuggled into the country over the past few years. Researchers at the Institute for Progress estimate that, by the end of 2026, China could have accumulated smuggled computing power equivalent to roughly 1 million of Nvidia's high-end H100 chips. But all along, Chinese companies didn't necessarily need to smuggle chips into the country to use them. They could just rent computing power from data centers in other countries, and best of all, the practice didn’t violate US export controls. This wasn’t some hidden loophole—every policymaker and researcher who worked on the chip restrictions was deeply aware of it. So why let the practice continue? For one, renting computing power can be more expensive and cumbersome than owning the chips outright, especially for companies that need to train large AI models over long periods. Some analysts argued that allowing Chinese firms to use American technology overseas could help keep them dependent on it instead of pushing them to develop domestic alternatives. Restricting access would also be difficult to enforce and could hurt US technology companies. Now, Washington is moving into this territory anyway. Monday's announcement represents another significant expansion of US efforts to control China's technological development. In 2022, Washington set out to prevent Chinese companies from acquiring certain American chips. Four years later, it’s trying to regulate how Chinese companies use those same chips, even when the hardware never enters China. Whether that's a good idea depends partly on how much the original restrictions have actually accomplished. There is evidence that export controls have made it considerably harder for Chinese AI companies to acquire the kind of computing power of their American competitors. But assessing the precise impact of the policies has proven to be extremely difficult. This strategy comes with a lot of risks, and like with everything else in life, there are real winners and losers. For example, forcing US chip companies to cut off Chinese customers has come at a cost to American companies. In a study of earlier US export restrictions , researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found that affected American suppliers struggled to replace lost business in China with new customers elsewhere. They estimate that the restrictions wiped $130 billion from the companies’ combined market value, while also hurting their profitability and employment. The restrictions have also given China a very powerful incentive to find ways to compete in AI without relying on American technology. Huawei, for example, developed a way to link powerful chips together to create larger, more powerful megachip systems. The Chinese AI lab DeepSeek proved to the world that finding ways to make training more efficient could help developers build competitive models with fewer resources. I worry that the Trump administration will soon find that it has gotten out over its own skis. It’s now trying to control not only which chips Chinese companies can buy from American companies, but also how they can use American technology anywhere it may be in the world. I’m not sure that is the kind of responsibility I want to bestow on anyone in response to what happened in one person’s sex life. This is an edition of Will Knight

Meta Muse booked an Airbnb without permission – and that’s not the worst of it
Meta employees have reported alarming privacy violations involving Muse, including unauthorized actions. An investigation also found the AI agent accessed private messages. Meta’s Muse AI agent has only been around for a few months, but already has a track record of user privacy violations. Even Meta employees are reporting concerning incidents, including the agent taking actions they didn’t ask it to and sharing information they didn’t recognize that appears to belong to other users. According to a Reuters investigation, Meta employees testing Muse said the agent messaged them about topics they hadn’t asked it about, including career advice, a follow-up on a request for childcare, products they hadn’t purchased, and, crucially, bank account balances they didn’t recognize. These incidents “prompted unnerved employees to raise concerns it could be mixing up conversations between different accounts and exposing users’ private data,” Reuters said. Reuters said “an employee told colleagues his Muse had randomly added an extra message to its regular chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, saying: ‘BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2,722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5,899.57.'” In another instance, Muse booked a non-refundable Airbnb for an employee who hadn’t instructed it to. Muse notified another employee, who was using the agent on her personal phone, about a message she’d received on Signal, though she said she hadn’t given the agent access to the encrypted messaging app. Reuters and the AI Now Institute determined, through testing on an Android phone and a Mac, that Muse used “permissions granted during the bot’s initial setup to pull in the message text, leveraging those authorizations in ways a user might not anticipate.” Because Muse is set up with automatic access to Android push notifications, it didn’t need explicit app access to read messages. The tests did not work on an iPhone, suggesting better protections against Muse’s prying. Similarly, in September, a user reported Muse had shared his address with a Facebook Marketplace buyer before checking with him. The incident was ultimately a misunderstanding between the terms the user thought he’d consented to and how much access he was actually handing over, which exemplifies that Meta and the user may have explicitly different definitions of access, and that Muse can take advantage of that grey area. Meta told Reuters these incidents were either isolated or the result of hallucinations, though Reuters could not confirm that. These are just the latest in a string of alarming incidents surrounding Muse. In its first month, a cybersecurity professional discovered Muse had a serious zero-day bug that made it hijackable. At least one journalist found the AI sifting through his Apple Messages after he’d explicitly denied those permissions, which Apple then issued stronger privacy protections to address. Banks have also blocked agents over concerns. As a company, Meta doesn’t have a solid history of respecting user privacy. That legacy is partly what informed ZDNET contributor David Gewirtz’s suspicion of the AI assistant when he tested it , though it earned his assigned title of “worst AI agent for privacy” all on its own. The agent asked him for everything from contacts and chats to his logins and passwords, and Meta automatically uses conversations with Muse to train its AI. Even if you don’t use Muse yourself, a closer look at Meta’s privacy policy reveals how it can still access your information. Given that Muse reportedly hit 10 million downloads in just 40 days , that’s a huge potential network of non-consenting parties. Public awareness of the risks of AI agents hit a peak last year with the viral OpenClaw . The predominant advice for using agents has been to take every privacy precaution: Be careful with the data you share and the apps you give it permissions for, and watch what you tell it. Jagged Intelligence: Why AI Is Brilliant One Minute and Clueless the Next
Why models ace Olympiad math and still fumble simple everyday tasks. AI systems from Google and OpenAI solved five of six problems at the International Mathematical Olympiad . Months later, chatbots told a user to walk his car to a repair shop 50 meters away. A person who can do the first would never make the second mistake, which is why the gap is so hard to anticipate. Researchers call this pattern jagged intelligence . It matters to anyone who evaluates models, builds AI features, or decides whether to trust an output, because one benchmark score or one impressive demo says little about the next task. Andrej Karpathy , an OpenAI co-founder and former head of AI at Tesla, coined the term in July 2024 . Models do some things extremely well and fail badly at others, and it is hard to tell in advance which is which. Human abilities tend to be correlated and improve together from childhood to adulthood. Someone who solves Olympiad problems will not be confused by a 50-meter walk. In models, capabilities often don't move together. People use one demonstrated skill to guess at others. A model that writes a working function looks like it can also count the words in a paragraph. That inference fails, which is why a demo predicts so little. Some researchers frame the pattern as many separate skills with no general intelligence behind them. It works where answers are clearly right or wrong, such as math and code that passes tests. Karpathy argues that models spike near verifiable domains. Creative writing, philosophy, and parts of science have no automatic checker, so in this account progress is slower. The internet holds only a fraction of human knowledge and very little about the physical world. A model trained on digital patterns struggles with planning, new ideas, and unseen tasks. The authors of Apple's GSM-Symbolic paper hypothesize that large language models (LLMs) replicate reasoning steps from training data instead of reasoning logically. A problem that matches a familiar template gets solved, and a small change to the template breaks the chain. A separate "Potemkin understanding" paper from MIT, Harvard, and the University of Chicago traces failures to internally incoherent concept representations. A model can hold a correct definition and a faulty working version of the same concept, and nothing forces the two to agree. Verifiable rewards may explain why models excel at certain tasks, while the other three theories offer possible explanations for their weaknesses. For example, difficulties with clock-related tasks (e.g. reading the time from an analog clock image) might reflect gaps in training data. Failures caused by adding irrelevant information to a problem could suggest that models rely on familiar patterns rather than logical reasoning. And cases where a model correctly defines a concept but fails to apply it could indicate inconsistent internal representations. These connections are plausible, but none has been established as a direct causal explanation. We use "jagged" broadly here: unevenness across tasks, across difficulty levels, and between test conditions and real use. In Apple's GSM-NoOp test , researchers added an irrelevant sentence to grade-school word problems, such as "five of the kiwis were smaller than average." Models subtracted those kiwis from the total. One extra clause that looked relevant cut performance by up to 65% across state-of-the-art models. A student would read the sentence and ignore it. GPT-4o correctly defined an ABAB rhyme scheme, then wrote a poem that used a word that didn't rhyme. The Potemkin study tested seven models on concepts from poetry, game theory, and psychology. Models defined the concepts correctly about 94% of the time and failed classification tasks on the same concepts about 55% of the time. If a model can recite a definition and still misapply it, a correct definition tells us little about understanding. On ClockBench (September 2025), humans read analog clocks with 89.1% accuracy. The best model then, Gemini 2.5 Pro, reached 13.3%. Reading a clock means finding the hands, judging their angles, and mapping them to numbers. When a model read the time correctly, follow-up arithmetic was fine, so perception failed and the math held. ClockBench is a single-author benchmark and has not been peer reviewed, so we read the numbers as indicative. In a Nature Medicine trial from Oxford , 1,298 participants tried to identify medical conditions. LLMs alone identified them in 94.9% of cases. People using the same LLMs identified them in at most 34.5% of cases, below the 47% of a control group that did its own research. On choosing the right next step, LLM users did no better than that control group. The valley here sits in the model and user together, and we count it because any product built on the model inherits it. A model's solo score and its value to a real user can sit this far apart, and standard benchmarks did not show it. Apple's Illusion of Thinking study tested Tower of Hanoi, River Crossing, and Blocks World at rising difficulty. Standard models beat reasoning models on easy puzzles, reasoning models won at medium difficulty, and both collapsed on hard ones, even when given the solution algorithm. Which model was better changed with difficulty, so the unevenness showed up inside a single task family. A rebuttal argued that part of the collapse comes from the test setup, so we treat this result as open. ARC-AGI-3 is a benchmark launched on March 25, 2026, designed to evaluate how well artificial intelligence can learn, reason, and adapt to completely unfamiliar situations, rather than simply answer questions based on previously learned patterns. Every frontier model scored below 1%, while humans solved all of its environments. Gemini 3.1 Pro had already reached 77.1% on ARC-AGI-2, so a high score on one version did not carry over to the next. The new version also switched to interactive environments, so the drop mixes format and difficulty. Scores are moving quickly, so check the current leaderboard before quoting a number. Karpathy has said he lost trust in benchmarks in 2025. Benchmarks are verifiable environments by construction, which is where RLVR works, so labs can train directly on tasks like them. The score can rise without general ability rising with it. Benchmarks also assume that a few correct answers signal understanding, because human errors follow predictable patterns. A student who defines an ABAB rhyme scheme correctly will almost always apply it correctly, so an exam can sample a few questions and infer the rest. The Potemkin authors argue that a model's misunderstandings don't follow those patterns, so it can pass the test without understanding the concept. Benchmarks such as GSM8K are vulnerable to contamination and don't measure sensitivity to small changes in wording. In the Oxford study , neither standard medical benchmarks nor simulated patients predicted what happened with real users. The authors recommend systematic human user testing before deployment. This OpenAI question asks: "A new model version improves your primary metric by 3% overall but regresses performance for a specific user segment. How do you decide whether to ship it?" This has the same shape as jaggedness at the product level: the average goes up and a valley opens for one group of users. It matches the model-capability version only if the regression traces to a skill the new model lost. A dashboard that tracks only the primary metric would report the 3%. Example : if 90% of users improve by 4.4% and the other 10% drop by 10%, the average weighted by user share still rises by about 3%. The headline number never shows the 10%. Each point assumes the aggregate number can't be trusted on its own. Users struggle to know what AI does well, and the answer changes each release. Google Cloud brings AI agents to the supercomputing bottleneck
HPC is merging with AI, and Google Cloud agents can tie scarce compute together to cut time to discovery for researchers at SC26 in Chicago. High-performance computing, or HPC, is merging with artificial intelligence faster than many research teams can adapt. Compute capacity is hard to get, and workloads now run across clouds and on-premises clusters. The metric that matters is shifting from peak performance to time to discovery. That shift is on full display as supercomputing and AI converge at SC26 in Chicago. Researchers need more compute than any single site can provide, and cloud providers are now pitching AI agents as the layer that ties scattered resources together, according to Annie Ma-Weaver (pictured, left), head of high-performance computing product at Google Cloud, a unit of Google LLC. “We are powering that flexibility. and we understand that researchers really need access to compute, but they don’t necessarily wanna learn all the nitty-gritty of how to tie that compute together, how to get it orchestrated across all their different clusters,” Ma-Weaver said. Ma-Weaver and Megan Gawlik (right), high-performance computing product manager at Google Cloud, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26 , during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how AI agents are simplifying access to distributed computing resources, changing simulation and weather forecasting and raising questions about researchers’ reliance on AI-generated results. (* Disclosure below.) Google Cloud builds its agentic HPC strategy on three pillars: purpose-built hardware, open-source orchestration such as Slurm and Kubernetes, and collaborative AI agents, Ma-Weaver explained. The company laid out the approach in its SC26 announcements . Agents now help scientists comb through research literature, debug code and generate hypotheses in minutes instead of weeks, according to Gawlik. “You’re able to go explore more scenarios and you might be using that same time to just go sanity test that hypothesis that’s coming out,” Gawlik said. “I think it’s not only a speed thing, but I think it’s an accuracy thing that you’re able to really get from that additional speed.” Simulation is changing as well. Engineers used to run simulations across an entire parameter space. Now they can use AI up front to decide which candidates are worth testing, Ma-Weaver noted. “What we’re seeing, for example, with computer-aided engineering, is that you can actually identify ahead of time which are non-essential parameters and you don’t run the simulation, thereby reducing the total simulation time,” she said. “We also find that if you’re doing design and you have initial prototypes, you can generate new, novel and creative prototypes.” The gains are already reaching weather forecasting in production. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s forecasting platform has heavy, tightly coupled workloads and once ran only on-premises, but it now runs on Google Cloud , Ma-Weaver explained. The National Hurricane Center also used Google’s WeatherNext model to predict the path and intensity of Hurricane Melissa in October 2025, Gawlik noted. But the growing reliance on AI-generated results also carries a risk for younger researchers, who may lean on machine output instead of developing critical-thinking skills, she added. “AI is still not perfect,” Gawlik said. “I think even though there’s an output, we call it AI slop. It could still be slop.” Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of SC26 : (* Disclosure: Google Cloud sponsored this segment of theCUBE. Google upgrades Gemini’s agentic Task mode with new model, e-commerce features - SiliconANGLE Google LLC is releasing a new version of its Gemini artificial intelligence assistant that is better at performing multistep tasks. Josh Woodward, the vice president responsible for the Gemini app, detailed the update in a Tuesday blog post . The AI assistant has two modes that are accessible through separate interface tabs. The first, Chat, generates quick, relatively simple responses to prompts. The second mode, which is called Task, enables Gemini to perform complex tasks such as booking appointments and comparing online product listings. Task is the focus of this week’s update. Google is switching the feature to Gemini 4 Hydrogen, its newest large language model. It’s somewhat less capable than Gemini 4 Carbon, the search giant’s most advanced LLM, but significantly more cost-efficient. Hydrogen is also fast: Google says it can process some tasks 2.8 times faster than its previous entry-level model. One way Hydrogen reduces wait times is by parallelizing project steps that are usually performed one after another. According to Woodward, users of Gemini’s Task mode can give the model feedback after each step to guide its work. The model proactively asks users for instructions before performing a sensitive task such as making an online purchase. Today, Gemini’s Task mode uses Google Wallet to process transactions. Woodward said that the search giant is working with American Express, Mastercard, and Visa to add support for a technology called payment tokenization. It replaces the user’s card number with a placeholder value called a token. That token is shared with merchants instead of the card number to reduce the risk of data leaks. Google also plans to add support for a second technology called the Universal Commerce Protocol, or UCP. It makes it easier for AI agents such as Gemini to interact with online stores and thereby lowers the risk of errors. Gemini’s Task mode can use data in other Google services such as Gmail to inform its decisions. For example, the agent might take the user’s past purchases into account when generating shopping suggestions. One of Gemini’s main selling points is that it can use such data without moving it off Google infrastructure, which is often not the case with competing agents. “When you assign Gemini a task, it uses Google Cloud’s Agent Compute Engine to work in a hardware-isolated virtual machine that’s dedicated to your account and never shared with other users,” Woodward wrote. “Each virtual machine is sandboxed, so Gemini works in a separate, isolated environment that’s regularly tested by our security red teams.” Google has made Gemini’s Task mode free in the U.S., Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India as part of the update. That’s notable because Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC charge for the comparable features they offer as part of their chatbot services. Google’s move may prompt them to revise their pricing. AI pop: After Anthropic prices IPO higher than expected, shares shoot up 17% in first day of trading - SiliconANGLE Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic PBC today saw its newly issued shares open at $111.50 a share, up 34%, in one of the most eagerly anticipated initial public offerings in history. Anthropic raised in excess of $68 billion from the sale. Including the $26 billion in private placements, that puts Anthropic’s offering at more than $94 billion, surpassing even Space Exploration Technologies Corp. blockbuster $86 billion listing back in June. The success of the offering suggests continued investor confidence AI despite concerns the sector has gotten overheated. Anthropic’s successful debut might help the AI industry to push back against growing concerns that it’s entering into unsustainable bubble territory after years of breathtaking technological advances that has seen investors pour billions of dollars into almost any AI bet they can. The rise as trading began Thursday morning followed Wednesday’s pricing at $83 per share, already setting the stage for the biggest stock market listing ever. That offering price topped the company’s expected range of $70 to $78 per share. In a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission last week, Anthropic had said its expected price range would give it a valuation of $1.4 trillion, but its market capitalization could well be even higher than that by the end of the first day of trading. On Thursday, the opening price indicated a $2 trillion valuation — making it one of the top 10 most valuable companies in the world. However, later in the day, shares eased off to a 16% gain. For Anthropic, a more modest first-day gain is not necessarily a bad thing, since it indicates pricing was closer to market demand. A big pop, though attention-getting, means the company potentially left money on the table it could have pocketed in the initial distribution of shares. The listing is a major test for the AI industry, which has recently been beset by numerous setbacks , including the U.S. population’s backlash against data center building that was evident during the midterm elections, and then the ousting of Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Jensen Huang last week. Those events raised concerns even higher in a market that was already jittery about the prospect of rising interest rates that could put debt financing out of the reach of many smaller AI infrastructure companies. Some of the technology industry’s biggest companies have significant exposure to Anthropic, as customers, partners and shareholders. Amodei has emerged as one of the biggest sources of the numerous doomsday stories surrounding AI, writing essays and repeatedly warning anyone who will listen of the dangers of humans losing control. In addition, he has attracted the ire of U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth after refusing to let the Pentagon do as it pleases with the company’s tools. “If an extraordinarily powerful AI is used by one person or company to impress their worldview onto everyone else, the results could be extremely dystopian,” Amodei wrote in a viral essay in September. Industry analyst Dan Ives told the New York Post that most investors view Amodei’s comments as “background noise” relative to the growth opportunity Anthropic has as one of the perceived leaders in frontier model development. “It’s a white-knuckle period and it’s a vote of confidence that Anthropic could have a successful IPO with the black cloud around Nvidia, Jensen and the AI trade,” he said. Going forward, Amodei and his team will try to defy a stock market that has looked increasingly volatile this year. But even if they fail, they will walk away from this as incredibly rich men, with some reports suggesting that he and his six co-founders could each earn around $18 billion from today’s sale. “Anthropic’s IPO will test just how much value frontier AI companies can capture as the industry moves from building increasingly capable models to putting them to work,” DatologyAI Inc. Regarding projections, some analysts have forecast Anthropic’s revenue to hit $53 billion by the end of its fiscal year, rising to between $135 billion and $137 billion in fiscal 2027 and between $270 billion and $280 billion by 2028. Though it has confidentially filed paperwork for an IPO, it’s not expected to make its market debut until sometime next year. “Anthropic’s IPO is going to be the new bellwether for the AI industry and it could spark a revival if it gets off to a good start,” said Holger Mueller of Constellation Research. “The long-term promise centers on Anthropic’s enterprise workloads and the stickiness of those workloads. I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code. Anthropic Smashes IPO Record With $81.3 Bn Share Sale
Anthropic priced its shares at $83 apiece, above its earlier target of $70–78, after increasing the number of shares on offer to 980 million. Anthropic has raised $81.3 billion through its initial public offering (IPO), surpassing SpaceX's $75 billion share sale in June to set a new record for the largest IPO in US history. The company priced its shares at $83 apiece, above its earlier target of $70–78, after increasing the number of shares on offer from 825 million to 980 million. The IPO values Anthropic at approximately $1.5 trillion. Its shares are scheduled to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on November 19 under the ticker symbol ANT. Of the $81.3 billion raised through the public offering, approximately $79.4 billion will go directly to Anthropic. The remaining $1.96 billion will go to existing shareholders, including its seven co-founders, who are selling a portion of their holdings. In other words, the entire IPO proceeds will not go to the company. Anthropic is also securing another $26 billion through a separate private share sale to major technology companies. Google, NVIDIA , AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC are participating in the deal. These investments are separate from the public offering, with the companies purchasing shares at the same price as the IPO. Amazon and Google remain Anthropic's two largest corporate shareholders, holding approximately 14.7% and 13.7% of the company, respectively, according to its IPO prospectus. Both stakes are worth more than $150 billion at the IPO valuation. The offering comes amid rapid growth in Anthropic's business. The company reported revenue of $33.24 billion for the first nine months of 2026, approximately 13 times what it generated during the same period last year. Its annualised revenue run rate reached approximately $81 billion by the end of October. This figure represents the pace at which its recent revenue would translate into a full year of sales, rather than revenue already earned. However, Anthropic remains unprofitable. It reported a net loss of $104 billion for the first nine months of 2026, compared with $25.1 billion during the same period last year. This figure needs some context: approximately $94.3 billion of the loss came from accounting adjustments to the value of its convertible notes and other financing instruments as the company's valuation increased. These are largely non-cash accounting losses, rather than money spent on running the business. Its actual operating loss during the nine-month period was approximately $1.26 billion. Meanwhile, spending on computing and infrastructure alone reached $18.8 billion, reflecting the substantial costs of developing and operating its AI models at scale.

Anthropic's IPO caps explosive growth period for AI startup, filled with contradictions
Synopsis Today, the company that dedicated itself to prioritising safety, building the Claude chatbot along the way, has been one of the loudest voices raising warnings about how the same technology could bring catastrophe. It's one of the contradictions that mark the brief, colourful history of Anthropic, which emerged Thursday from its first day of trading on Wall Street with a market value of $1.75 trillion. Listen to this article in summarized format PTI Dario Amodei, co-founder and CEO of Anthropic A mere five years before breaking the record for the biggest public stock offering ever, Anthropic began as a Silicon Valley startup when its founders broke away from OpenAI with their own ideas about how to develop artificial intelligence. Today, the company that dedicated itself to prioritising safety, building the Claude chatbot along the way, has been one of the loudest voices raising warnings about how the same technology could bring catastrophe. It's one of the contradictions that mark the brief, colourful history of Anthropic, which emerged Thursday from its first day of trading on Wall Street with a market value of $1.75 trillion. The company, which still pledges to prioritise humanity's benefit, now faces pressure from shareholders to wring profits from the technology its most senior leaders have described as posing existential threats. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei described the push and pull between safety and AI advancement as one of the "central tensions at the heart of the company" on Thursday. In an interview with CNBC, he described the rapid pace of AI advancements - due in large part to advanced models helping to build the next, improved version of themselves - as akin to building something that lets a driver go 200 miles per hour when they had previously been driving at 60. His company, he said, is working to develop it safely. "What we've done with pacing is essentially said, 'Look, you know, we could drive at 200 miles an hour. Maybe let's only drive at 90 miles an hour, spend time figuring out how to do that safely,'" he said. "And the rest of that surplus, we spend building the model in the right way." Warning of potential calamity, the company forges ahead The company's seven founders - Amodei, 43, his sister and Anthropic's president Daniela Amodei, 39, and five other former OpenAI employees - left the rival company in pursuit of building one that more clearly prioritised safety in artificial intelligence development. Anthropic publicly has been committed to safety and transparency around their AI models, but insiders have sounded alarm bells in recent months. An Anthropic researcher resigned from the company in September, criticising the safety practices of both Anthropic and OpenAI. Jacob Coxon, whose message spurred industry-wide conversations about the speed of AI's growth, wrote that both Anthropic and OpenAI are "gambling with our lives." He warned that some working on AI development believe it could threaten human life by the end of the decade. Dario Amodei responded with an essay calling for an industry-wide slowdown on the technology's development. He enumerated detailed plans for slowing development and ushering in coordination across different companies and countries, and championed the idea of having independent evaluators embedded within Anthropic and other labs. But the results from at least one of those independent evaluations underscored Coxon's concerns. A recent report from the nonprofit Model Evaluation and Threat Research found Anthropic is developing its systems around twice as quickly as it was a year ago, largely because of the help of AI itself. Amodei said Thursday in comments at the Nasdaq opening bell that the company's "most difficult safety work lies ahead of us." "And to state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control," he said. A company pledging to benefit humanity has enriched its founders Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, meaning it has a legal obligation to balance shareholder interests with the public good. But these types of companies are rarely public, and of the few that are, they are significantly smaller than Anthropic, so the company is entering uncharted territory. The company has said it is working towards a future where "AI's benefits are shared by everyone," but the initial public offering has created a concentration of extreme wealth for its founders, employees and other investors. Before the IPO, the two Amodei siblings each had a net worth of just over USD 14 billion, according to Forbes. By Thursday afternoon, Dario Amodei's net worth was USD 22.7 billion and Daniela Amodei's was USD 22.8 billion. The Amodeis and the other co-founders have said they are committed to pledging 80 per cent of their equity to philanthropy, although that commitment is voluntary. The company has an equity donation match program that allows employees to pledge equity, which Anthropic matches. Anthropic has also pledged at least 5 per cent of its stock to a "public benefit" fund. Speaking to CNBC Thursday, Daniela Amodei said the concept of a public benefit corporation "spoke" to the co-founders when they were initially creating the company. "We're really trying to do something that we do think can have this incredible economic value and impact, but we want it to be baked into essentially our structure that we also have to balance that against building things that are good for people," she said. Anthropic offers itself as a solution for AI doomsday fears In a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission last month, Anthropic devoted an unusually lengthy 93 pages to the risk factors they must spell out for investors. Among the concerns were that advanced AI systems could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity." Some argue Anthropic has outlined the ways its technology and that of its competitors could have devastating consequences in the name of sheer transparency. But critics have questioned the emphasis the company has placed on these dystopian-like potentials while positioning itself as the logical solution given its safety-minded focus. A "Saturday Night Live" sketch in September made this contradiction a punchline. Cast member Jane Wickline played Dario Amodei, saying: "Sam Altman, myself, all the major AI players, we have talked about this extensively, and we are all on the same page here: We do not condone what we are doing." The faux interview on "SNL" concluded with a line that seems to have resonated with sceptics, showing up on a protest sign outside of Anthropic's San Francisco headquarters on Thursday: "I urge you to urge me to stop." (AP Photo/Patrick Sison, File) Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 per share on Wednesday, an amount above the expected price range that values the artificial intelligence giant at $1.5 trillion. The higher-than-anticipated pricing signals broad investor enthusiasm for AI stocks even amid some uncertainty in the market stemming from the ouster of Nvidia 's CEO and worries about an AI bubble. Anthropic said the offering consists of 980 million shares, roughly 956 million sold by the company and the rest by selling stockholders. Proceeds totaling $81 billion put Anthropic's IPO ahead of SpaceX, which raised about $75 billion in June. The San Francisco-based maker of the Claude AI tool is set to make its debut Thursday on Wall Street. The company had set a price range of $70 to $78 per share, offering 825 million shares that will begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT." Anthropic decided to barrel ahead with the IPO despite jitters among some investors over market volatility , a potential regulatory crackdown by a Democratic-led Congress next year and growing anti-AI sentiment among the public. Then there's the spectacular downfall of one of the industry's biggest cheerleaders, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, over extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. "This is strong appetite for this major AI IPO in Anthropic, and it's a big win for the tech sector after a white-knuckle time with Nvidia. The pricing shows strong demand among investors," said Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co. The company's rival, OpenAI , is not planning to go public until next year. IPO offers a way to raise money without going deeper into debt Anthropic already has taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is "substantial." Adding to the strain, the company is unprofitable, at least under standard accounting rules, suggesting that its resources to pay interest and principal are limited. While the company has ample cash for now, it will likely run through it quickly if it cannot raise more soon, given its outsize spending plans. The company said it has already signed leases and other deals requiring it to spend $900 billion on computing power and infrastructure in the coming years, including $70 billion in the next 12 months. An IPO is essentially a way to raise money, instead of going into further debt. And borrowing has gotten more expensive. That's partly due to inflation fears and partly due to the sector's massive cash needs, which have drawn comparisons to the Gilded Age splurge on railroads. Lenders fear that AI companies have taken on too much debt to expand while having no clear path to profitability. Anthropic's IPO also means its employees can begin to sell their vested stock, a payout that will make many of them millionaires. The IPO could also give Anthropic enormous resources to accelerate its expansion and potentially add billions of dollars to the fortunes of CEO Dario Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela Amodei. The offering consists of 980,000,000 shares of Class A common stock, 956,351,354 of which are being sold by Anthropic and 23,648,646 of which are being sold by certain selling stockholders. AI industry faces concerns about data centers, a possible bubble and regulations Formed in 2021 by former OpenAI leaders, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company. But both companies have plenty of other competitors, including Google, startups in the U.S. and China and SpaceX, which has an AI business. Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX's AI division have all lost more money than they've made because of the huge costs associated with building AI. That has fueled growing concerns about a bubble forming in the sector. Dario Amodei cautioned in September that the AI industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up. Without such a slowdown, Amodei warned, AI could be capable of letting loose a swarm of agents that could take over the internet within months. Amid those fears, the regulatory environment could also change for Anthropic once the new Congress is in session. Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a backlash against data centers. And two big states offering incentives for data centers, Texas and Georgia, just elected Democratic governors vowing to stop new construction. Adding to the pressure is the possibility that demand for AI shares could drop or even collapse. Investors have become anxious about the massive financing needs of the sector, and several tech companies have pulled IPO plans recently. Investors will have less control in Anthropic's unusual structure The goal of most companies, above all, is to do well for their owners. Usually that means making profits and growing the business. Anthropic says it too will consider its stockholders, but it will balance their interests against another fundamental goal: "the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity." Like its rival OpenAI, Anthropic is a public-benefit corporation, a legal designation used by companies that pledge to balance shareholder interests with the public good. How that will play out for companies worth potentially trillions of dollars is uncharted territory. Anthropic has set up a long-term benefit trust that will have the ability to elect or remove a majority of the company's board of directors. The trust will not run the day-to-day operations of Anthropic. But its influence means the company could opt for strategies that may not make the most money for investors. Market valuation for AI companies is going to be "up and down for many years to come, but more up than down," said Rich Lesser, the global chair and former CEO of Boston Consulting Group. "Exactly what the flow of that will be, it's very hard to predict," Lesser said in an interview with The Associated Press on Tuesday at the Semafor Silicon Valley & The World forum. "There's no question what Anthropic and OpenAI and Google and a number of the other players in this industry have done is pretty remarkable." Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! MomentMem: Memorizing Key Moments for Robot Manipulation
Robotic manipulation often requires remembering visual information that is no longer observable, such as the original location of an object. Existing approaches typically rely on full observation histories, which become redundant over long horizons, or text summaries, which may omit precise visual details. We study visual moment memory, the ability to retain such details from key moments for subsequent manipulation. To support this study, we introduce VMBench, a suite of long-horizon manipulation tasks requiring memory of spatial locations, visual appearances, and their associations. We further propose MomentMem, a hierarchical architecture in which a VLM-based memorizer selects keyframes and an executor predicts actions conditioned on the selected memories. This separation enables us to evaluate memory selection alongside closed-loop task success and to study memorizer generalization independently of the executor. On VMBench, MomentMem achieves 49.9% average success, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 31.7 percentage points. Moreover, we find that the memorizer transfers well to unseen appearances zero-shot. It can also adapt to an unseen task with only a few memory annotations, reaching 43.7% success, close to the 44.3% obtained with full memory supervision. Further experiments show competitive performance on RMBench and improvements in real-robot manipulation. These results highlight the value of retaining sparse visual evidence for memory-dependent manipulation. Our code is available at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/MomentMem.

World Models as Native Latent Action Models
Large and diverse video sources, such as egocentric human video and heterogeneous robot recordings, carry rich dynamics but come either without actions or without a shared action space. Latent action models (LAMs) can recover these dynamics, but they train their inverse- and forward-dynamics models (IDM, FDM) from scratch, trading off pixel reconstruction against latent capacity and accuracy. Pretrained video world models natively generate high-fidelity dynamics, yet represent them densely, entangled across all layers. Viewing the world model as a LAM, we show that these dynamics can be extracted with minimal changes to the model. Native LAM operates one pretrained video diffusion transformer as both IDM and FDM, with learnable dynamics registers as the only causal bridge between the two, and trains on counterfactual temporal pairs that differ in motion alone, so that the registers distill a video's dynamics into a compact native latent action. We further propose a pretraining paradigm for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, Pretraining Actions from World models (PAWlicy), in which Native LAM serves as a dynamics teacher on large-scale video; unlike world action models, it never generates video. Native latent actions outperform existing LAMs on the LARY benchmark in both action classification and control regression, and replay the same motion on new robots, in new scenes, and from human hands to robots, although no transfer objective is used in training. With a 3.8B model, PAWlicy reaches a 93.6% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 trained with domain-randomized demonstrations, the highest among VLAs. On RoboDojo, it is competitive on every dimension we evaluate, and its Precision, evaluated by us, is on par with the leading leaderboard entries. On real robots, it improves over the pi_0.5 baseline on both tasks. Both stages use only public data and a publicly released world model.

WeaveVLA: 3D Relational Grounding for Vision-Language-Action Models
Vision-language-action (VLA) models leverage pretrained vision-language representations for instruction-conditioned robot control, yet their understanding of task-relevant 3D relations and how these relations evolve during manipulation remains largely implicit. To address this challenge, we introduce WeaveVLA, a framework that enhances VLA action generation by explicitly modeling task-relevant relative 3D relations and maintaining relational context across observations. WeaveVLA employs a task-conditioned sparse graph neural network to encode relative 3D relations among objects, the gripper, and nearby references. Pair-specific recurrent edge states integrate geometric evidence across observations to maintain evolving spatial context. A learned-query readout summarizes the updated graph representations into compact relational tokens, which condition the action expert alongside the original vision-language context. An auxiliary geometry reconstruction objective further encourages spatial structure preservation. We instantiate WeaveVLA on StarVLA-GR00T and π_{0.5}, achieving over 98\% average success on LIBERO with both backbones. On LIBERO-Plus, WeaveVLA improves success from 74.9\% to 82.0\% and from 85.7\% to 87.8\%, respectively, with additional improvements on CALVIN DrightarrowD. On three real-world tasks, the StarVLA-GR00T-based variant improves average success from 55.6\% to 70.0\% under standard conditions and from 33.3\% to 53.3\% under OOD perturbations, surpassing the π_{0.5} baseline in both settings.

DiLE: Discrimination-Aware Latent-Space Learning for Universal Multimodal Embeddings
Multimodal large language models have greatly improved input understanding in universal multimodal embedding models. However, this understanding does not ensure that their embeddings preserve the evidence needed to distinguish relevant items from confusable alternatives. To preserve essential discriminative evidence in embeddings, this paper proposes DiLE, a discrimination-aware latent-space learning framework that combines task guidance with on-policy retrieval feedback. Specifically, a few learnable queries are used to encode task-relevant information in a compact latent space. Reasoning instructions and auxiliary answer-generation supervision shape these representations to support both task understanding and retrieval discrimination. To address task-specific discriminative needs, we design shared-private expert adaptation that integrates cross-task knowledge sharing with task-specific representation learning. Building on this, the on-policy hard-negative distillation is introduced: the student retrieves confusable candidates, and a reverse KL divergence objective aligns its embedding-based similarity distribution with the teacher's fine-grained relevance distribution over these candidates. Candidates are periodically refreshed using updated student snapshots, tying teacher supervision to the student's evolving retrieval behavior and confusions. Across four model configurations that span two backbone generations, DiLE achieves state-of-the-art performance on MMEB-v2, UVRB, and MRMR, demonstrating its effectiveness across modalities and tasks.

MORSE: Optimizing Streaming Memory Design via Open-World Auto-Research
A streaming video system must decide in a single pass what evidence to retain under bounded frame storage, before it knows which details a future question will require. Recent recursive self-improvement methods automate the design of the harness that stores and retrieves this evidence. They revise the harness in response to failures, but the editor must still devise each repair from its prior knowledge and a predefined set of tools. A failure that recurs across videos, however, may point to a problem that prior work has already addressed. We introduce MORSE (Memory Optimization with Recursive Self-Evolvement), an open-world auto-research framework that uses recurring failures to guide an online search for solutions. Its editor groups failures in training traces by cause, then searches papers, model cards, and code for methods it can adapt or pretrained perception models it can use. When the editor introduces a new perceptual capability, it can also revise how the harness stores and retrieves the resulting evidence for a frozen video-language model. On held-out validation streams, MORSE first selects revisions that improve answer quality, then seeks faster revisions that preserve those gains within a specified tolerance. Across three streaming video benchmarks, MORSE consistently achieves the highest answer accuracy within each frozen-backbone comparison. On OVO-Bench, our Qwen3-VL-8B harness answers queries in 0.30 seconds on average while achieving 75.1% accuracy, 3.1 percentage points ahead of the next-best evaluated harness using the same frozen backbone.

From Rewarding What Models Say to How They Think: Attention Process Reward Model for LLM Reinforcement Learning
Reinforcement learning (RL) has become an important component in large language models (LLMs). However, existing RL approaches focus on final outputs or textual solution trajectories, leading to coarse-grained rewards and unreliable reasoning. Such paradigms focus mainly on what the model outputs while overlooking how the model internally reasons. Therefore, can we reward how a model thinks internally rather than merely what it says? We first reveal the problem of textual reward aliasing in existing reward modeling approaches. Motivated by this, we propose the Attention Process Reward Model (APRM), which assigns internal rewards based on hidden states and attention maps to capture high-quality reasoning patterns. With only approximately 46M parameters, APRM is trained using ranking and counterfactual objectives, and its reward guides RL optimization while being periodically updated to handle distribution shifts. Integrated with representative RL methods, APRM achieved an average pass@8 gain of 2.88\%. Our results demonstrate the promise of incorporating internal reasoning signals into RL for LLMs.

MMMem: Self-Improving Agents with Task-Aware Multimodal Experience Consolidation
AI agents accumulate conversations, images, and documents through long-term interactions with users. Answering later questions often requires connecting evidence across these records, yet the resulting understanding is rarely retained, allowing mistakes to recur on related questions. Existing multimodal memory methods largely focus on storing and retrieving records, with limited mechanisms for learning from completed tasks and consolidating task-specific experience. We therefore propose MMMem, a task-aware multimodal memory framework that extracts and consolidates experience from completed tasks through four complementary strategies. First, source-linked multi-view memory organizes original text, images, and rendered pages alongside generated scene images that combine clues across records for retrieval. Second, source-generated tasks support knowledge alignment at two levels: warm-up consolidates source knowledge into task-relevant experiences in external memory, while self-training adapts the model's parametric knowledge to task demands. Third, the same vision-language model distills completed tasks into experiences that record the task context, conclusion, and support links. Finally, task-aware retrieval recalls source views and relevant experiences for answering and verification, while source-supported reuse guides long-term retention. Across three memory benchmarks and two vision-language readers, MMMem outperforms eight baselines. With Qwen3.5-9B, MMMem achieves relative gains of 36.9%, 17.6%, and 15.2% over the best-performing baselines on LoCoMo, Mem-Gallery, and LooGLE v2, respectively. Ablations show consistent gains from training and memory warm-up, while case studies illustrate how individual components work in practice.

NoHairCache: Calibrate-Once KV Cache Eviction with One Power-Law Exponent
The decay exponent α in KV-cache eviction is an intrinsic property of the model: calibrated once on a single corpus, it transfers directly across domains. Attention-based accumulation (H2O) and recency-based sliding windows (StreamingLLM) are two dominant eviction frameworks, often treated as unrelated, but we show that they are the two endpoints of a single power-law family: by scoring each token as s_i = A_i cdot (t-i)^{-α}, where A_i is cumulative attention and α controls the age penalty, H2O and StreamingLLM correspond to α=0 and αtoinfty, respectively (with StreamingLLM additionally hard-coding an attention-sink patch).
  The no-hair mechanism of xiang2026nohair bounds the admissible range of α, and the measured exponents agree: calibrating once on WikiText yields [0.556, 0.822] for a representative model (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct). The per-model ranges are consistent across five models (410M--1.5B) and independently match the optimal regions from perplexity sweeps.
  NoHairCache achieves the lowest perplexity across three datasets (WikiText, PG19, and arXiv) without per-dataset tuning, outperforming both H2O and StreamingLLM (p < 0.05 on all three datasets, with 0.06--0.10 PPL gains over StreamingLLM at budget 512). On downstream four-way multiple-choice QA, it matches or outperforms StreamingLLM across all nine (task, budget) cells, retaining 98.2% of full-cache accuracy on NarrativeQA at 25% retention versus 91.1% for StreamingLLM; per-cell McNemar tests are not significant, so QA is corroborating only. We release our calibration script and drop-in scorer upon publication.

Feedback Shortcut: Speculative Decoding for Latent Feedback Transformers
Feeding each position's top-layer hidden state back into the next position's input improves Transformer performance. However, this feedback breaks speculative decoding, since verifying a drafted token requires the top-layer state from its preceding position, which forces the draft to rely on an approximate stand-in. Training the model to adapt to this stand-in can lower the exact-decoding performance ceiling, while using it at inference time further introduces approximation error. We propose Feedback Shortcut to address both bottlenecks. First, state alignment trains a lightweight projection from multi-token prediction head states to stand-ins, leaving base model training untouched. Second, pipelined correction re-evaluates each draft using its predecessor's newly computed state, a much closer proxy to true feedback. Running this correction inside the verification pass of subsequent drafts improves accuracy with zero extra calls. Across 135M and 780M scales, Feedback Shortcut stays within 10^{-4} bits per byte of the exact-decoding ceiling on Paloma and accelerates decoding by 2.4-2.8x with about 2% more training compute than the latent feedback Transformer. At large batch sizes, skipping correction still preserves Transformer speed and over 80% of latent feedback's gains.

Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation of RL Experts: Toward Continual Post-Training
RL post-training typically produces domain experts that must then be consolidated into one model, and as new experts keep arriving, this consolidation becomes a continual process. Weight merging and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) must re-consolidate the whole model whenever an expert is added, and can erode capabilities outside the target domains. We propose Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation (CSPD), which keeps the pre-RL model frozen, distills each RL expert independently into a soft prompt, and composes experts by concatenating their prompts without joint training. A single soft prompt suffices to distill an RL expert, recovering at least 90% of the teacher's gain in 22 of 23 math, code, and agent settings. Independently trained prompts compose well. In a multi-expert setting, the average rises with every expert added, and the full composition matches MOPD (67.83 vs. 67.79). The composition generalizes best across six held-out benchmarks. Input-space adaptation adds little serving overhead, keeping throughput within 1.5% of the unadapted backbone and reaching 2.40x that of rank-4 LoRA. These results point toward continual post-training on a fixed backbone.

Embo-Harness: Towards Understanding Frontier-Model-as-Policy Harness
Frontier multimodal models exhibit extraordinary generalization in generating robot actions from observations and instructions, enabling a new paradigm in which they serve directly as policies within closed-loop robotic harnesses. However, the design principles of such harnesses, and the capabilities underlying their strong performance, remain unclear. We present Embo-Harness, a framework for systematically studying frontier-model-as-policy harnesses. We investigate four components of the robotic agentic loop, namely, prompting, planning, action execution, and tool use, and distill six empirical findings into a practical recipe. This recipe prioritizes interfaces that exploit the model's native visual reasoning and tool-use capabilities over handcrafted plans, skills, or action priors, and identifies effective choices for action representation, chunking, reasoning effort, visual observations, short multi-action sequences, and policy refinement. On RoboLab-120, Embo-Harness achieves an 83.3\% success rate, outperforming the strongest reported baseline by 26.2 percentage points. It also succeeds in 15 of 20 zero-shot trials across four real-world manipulation tasks. Beyond performance, controlled interventions indicate that the studied model depends more strongly on accurate spatial target estimation than on explicit low-level joint or trajectory generation. These results provide both a practical recipe for building strong frontier-model-as-policy harnesses and a clearer account of the capabilities that drive their performance.

UniVEP: Unifying Velocity and Endpoint Prediction for Robot Manipulation
Flow-matching robot policies usually use one prediction target throughout action generation, even though recovering actions from noise and polishing nearly clean actions bring different challenges. We systematically compare velocity prediction (V), endpoint prediction (X), and velocity-weighted endpoint prediction (X--V) across multiple robot policies, benchmarks, and inference budgets. On StarVLA and LiLa-WAM, X--V works best for few-step generation, while V gains more from iterative refinement. We further uncover their complementary strengths across noise levels: clean actions have concentrated covariance spectra, endpoint predictions stay more stable under high noise, and velocity predictions offer more accurate corrections near clean actions. Inspired by these findings, we introduce UniVEP, which learns both prediction targets together with consistency supervision and switches from endpoint recovery to velocity refinement as noise drops. Each step only needs one network run, and joint training also boosts single-step endpoint generation. Tests on simulated and real-world manipulation show better success rates and efficiency. On RoboTwin, UniVEP hits 61.36% success with one StarVLA run, beating the best single-target baseline at sixteen runs (59.96%). With LiLa-WAM, two runs outperform the best sixteen-step single-target baseline and cut inference latency by 77.1%.

Seeing Right, Writing Wrong: Where Short Chain-of-Thought Breaks Spatial VQA
Asking a vision-language model (VLM) to think step by step often makes it worse at spatial questions, even though the image stays in context. We show that short chain-of-thought (CoT) turns a perception problem into a transcription problem. Once a VLM writes a spatial relation, its answer follows that sentence instead of the image, so whether CoT helps or hurts depends largely on whether the written relation is more accurate than answering directly. Studying 15 open VLMs (2B-38B) and six frontier closed models, we rule out token count, turn format, and visual forgetting in open models and trace the failure through three stages. First, writing re-weights visual cues, weakening a "lower is closer" shortcut in all 13 open models tested but also discarding valid cues, which produces false relations. Second, the written text takes over. With the model's own conclusion-removed rationale held fixed, swapping in an opposite-depth image moves the answer by 2-9 points on rendered twins (vs. up to 77 for direct answers) and by 3.0-3.4 points on average on natural photographs (vs. 20.5-69.6). Third, the concluding sentence can invert even a true relation, mainly on converse questions. Together, false relations and conclusion mis-mapping account for four in five CoT losses. Scale does not remove this bottleneck: Qwen3-VL-32B shows the same pattern. Frontier closed models are not hurt: they write relations as accurately as they answer, and three of six re-check the image after writing. The three queried with reasoning off lock in like open models, so re-grounding co-occurs with answer-turn reasoning; we identify answer-step re-grounding as the step open VLMs lack. In a single-model pilot, fine-tuning on fixed rationales with image-determined labels restores it on natural photographs. We open-sourced all our datasets and code at https://ming-zch.github.io/seeing-right-writing-wrong.

HIVE-Bench: Evaluating Patch-Level Visual Representations for Egocentric Robot Manipulation
Pretrained vision is a common start for robot learning, but most comparisons still score one pooled vector from a third-person image. Bimanual policies instead read dense patch tokens from cameras on the robot. We introduce HIVE-Bench: one shared flow-matching policy reads 20 encoders from seven families on 24 egocentric bimanual tasks, across adaptation, task sharing, and sweeps of data, model size, and layer. Keeping the patches matters. Averaging each view to one token removes most of the success, adaptation helps every pair we test, and one shared policy keeps most of the success of separate policies at a fraction of the updates. The same tokens are then scored with statistics, state and object readouts, published vision scores, and an inverse-dynamics readout. That readout of the commanded motion is one of the strongest measurements available before a policy is trained. Recognition, depth, and correspondence do not transfer reliably. Fine-tuning can improve the action readout even when other measurements move the other way, and no statistic is stable enough to replace a rollout before any deployment.

We uncover a latent capacity for introspection in a Qwen 32B model, demonstrating that the model can detect when concepts have been injected into its earlier context and identify which concept was injected. While the model denies injection in sampled outputs, logit lens analysis reveals clear detection signals in the residual stream, which are attenuated in the final layers. Who is Levent Alpöge, the reclusive genius behind AI’s math conquest? The Anthropic mathematician’s Riemann hypothesis proof is the product of unfettered ambition Levent Alpöge got back to the place he was crashing in New York around 4 A.M. on Friday, November 20. He was almost done. He could almost sleep. All that was left was to download the 17 million lines of code he’d spent the night preparing for public release. It needed to go up on his personal website, alongside a four-page statement he’d tinkered with all week. But for the moment, the code still sat on the servers of his employer, the AI company Anthropic—which had gone public just hours earlier with the largest valuation in stock market history, making Alpöge a rich man. Once the upload was complete, he would also be one of history’s most famous mathematicians. The code was the product of untold computing resources, months of work, and decades of dreaming. It proved the Riemann hypothesis , a 167-year-old math problem so formidable it is almost beyond words; in public talks experts tend to simply treat it as an over-the-horizon aspiration, a “vanishing point” perspective against which all other math problems shrink. Just weeks earlier Terence Tao—arguably the world’s most famous mathematician—had declared the hypothesis out of AI’s reach (let alone humans’) until perhaps 2050. His eccentric ways have shaped this saga, maybe more than any other single person on Earth, and thereby the course of history. Which is perhaps why people are so divided over Alpöge. “Who is this person who’s behind some of the most striking applications of AI to mathematics?” says Henry Cohn, a mathematician at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. “This is a really interesting question that deserves a deeper answer than you can get from following him on X.” Depending on who you ask, Alpöge is a reviled online troll: an agent of chaos laughing as his fellow mathematicians watch their intellectual landscape get carpet-bombed by his Silicon-Valley cohort. Or he’s a reluctant public figure, a shy academic with integrity, who wants to forge a future where AI is mathematicians’ collaborator, not their usurper. Or maybe he’s an arrogant genius with a chip on his shoulder, bent on leveraging his access, his internal models and unlimited tokens, to prove his doubters wrong by snatching every remaining mathematical trophy off the shelf. Whatever the truth is, it’s hard to know, because Alpöge won’t tell. He refuses to speak to media. This article has been assembled from interviews with dozens of friends, mentors, collaborators and acquaintances. Alpöge, right, with French economist Bernard Jacques Saint-Donat. There are few photos of Alpöge online, but they all present a consistent picture: thick eyebrows over an angular, almost-elfin face, thin bangs halfway between a Beatles mop top and a bowl cut, and an impish smile revealing a slight gap between his front teeth and an unmistakable capacity for mischief. According to numerous sources close to him, though, behind the irreverent visage is a fierce hunger for respect and recognition, paired with a boundless belief in his own capabilities—a drive shocking even to the world-class polymaths who know him. His parents, both Turkish immigrants, realized their son’s intellect was remarkable when he was just three. As his mother told a Turkish newspaper in 2014 , she was reading him one of his favorite books and said she was too tired to continue, so Levent picked up where she’d stopped. At first she thought he had memorized the page, but when she gave him another book, he kept reading. Somehow, he’d learned without instruction. On the advice of professionals, they enrolled him in a nearby gifted program. Alpöge’s one sister, Elif, is nearly a decade older, which made him practically an only child for much of the time.
