AI Solved Math’s Most Famous Problem. Now Humans Are Struggling to Understand It
It will take mathematicians months to understand the “alien” 17-million-line solution an Anthropic researcher produced for the Riemann hypothesis. Mathematicians are struggling to decode a 17-million-line solution to their field’s most famous problem, published by an Anthropic researcher on Friday. Levent Alpöge released a proof in the programming language Lean of the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis, which he had created with Claude. While the conjecture, which describes how prime numbers are distributed, is widely assumed to be true , many mathematicians have tried and failed to definitively show this, and the problem has become something of a holy grail of number theory. Since Alpöge published his proof, more than 200 people have been collaborating to verify it. On Saturday, the nonprofit the Lean Focused Research Organization and volunteer-led organization Mathlib said on Saturday they have “full confidence” that the proof is sound. The problem is formulated correctly and the code compiles, they confirmed. Now, “we look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the new ideas in this proof,” they wrote. Lean proofs are written to be checked by machine, while mathematical papers are written to explain the results to the community so that they can be reviewed and advanced. But Alpöge hasn’t released the paper version, which clocks in at 250,000 pages and is, in his own estimation, a “travesty of slop.” (On Monday, he added in an X post that the Lean proof “is full of garbage obviously” but that it still “compiles.” He also said that the 250,000 pages was a “joke … I find big number [sic] extremely hilarious.”) That’s left mathematicians to their own devices as they try to decipher what new findings they can obtain and build from the result. “Knowing there is a proof is one thing,” Abhishek Saha, a professor of mathematics at Queen Mary University of London, tells WIRED, “but when we understand the proof, that would allow us to actually go beyond what has happened, to build new branches of mathematics perhaps or formulate the next conjecture to push the horizon further.” Saha reckons the community effort should be able to simplify the result into a human-readable form of under 10,000, if not 1,000, pages. But complicating this feat is the fact that the proof appears to draw on many advanced branches of number theory in a long and “incredibly counterintuitive” argument. “I don't think this kind of proof would ever come from a human,” says Saha, “but AIs can do something completely different and almost alien, and that breaks our intuition about how very difficult mathematical results might come about.” He was shocked to see even his own corner of number theory utilized by the proof, and has since been trying to understand how. Saha has been using OpenAI’s Astra model to convert sections of the Lean proof into more digestible formats, such as single-page posters like those presented at conferences and shorter documents. But there’s a limit to that approach. “It may well be that no single person has the expertise to understand in detail every part of the proof,” he says. More than 60 other individuals are using AI agents to try to translate the Lean lines into understandable ideas on Principia Math, a collaborative platform designed to facilitate the understanding of AI breakthroughs. So far, they have done this for more than 3,000 pieces of the Lean proof, though platform chief executive officer Anton Shakov expects it will take mathematicians months before they have a good conceptual understanding of the proof Alpöge produced with Claude in roughly six weeks. “I personally believe the picture we will get in the end, once the ideas of this proof have been properly understood, will be astoundingly beautiful," he tells WIRED. Independent mathematicians have already understood and written up one smaller result to have come out of Alpöge’s proof. AI labs have previously been criticized for rushing to publish breakthrough mathematical results , claiming glory while leaving the academic community to digest the results—and clean up mistakes. “No human being can reasonably claim to be responsible for, or even to understand, such a document,” the Association for Human Mathematics, a group of more than 1,000 mathematicians founded in September, wrote in a statement on Friday of the 17-million-line opus. It complained that Alpöge’s announcement “builds upon over a century of human work, but fails to advance mathematical understanding in the same way.” Alpöge, who before joining Anthropic was a researcher at Harvard University, acknowledged on Friday what an “extraordinary” situation it was to present “the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighborhood around its mathematics,” and wrote that he would try his best to help digest the proof, including by writing it up properly. But having had to hold off from making the announcement ahead of Anthropic’s initial public offering on Thursday, “I just could not live if I waited even longer,” he wrote. Anthropic rival OpenAI in October proved a weaker version of the problem, called the quasi-Riemann hypothesis. Alpöge had been scooped by OpenAI in September on another Millennium Prize Problem concerning the Navier-Stokes equations, which describe fluid motion. When the company said it had solved part of the problem, Alpöge’s collaborator, New York University professor Tristan Buckmaster, claimed OpenAI had rushed ahead to beat the pair to it after becoming aware of his work. The pair also announced on Friday that they had completed the remaining unsolved parts of the Navier-Stokes problem.

One of mathematics’ most famous unsolved problems may have just been cracked. The proof isn’t a paper, though. It’s a codebase.Levent Alpöge, a number theorist One of mathematics’ most famous unsolved problems may have just been cracked. The proof isn’t a paper, though. It’s a codebase. Levent Alpöge, a number theorist affiliated with Anthropic and the Harvard Society of Fellows, has released a formal proof of the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis. He built it with Claude, Anthropic’s AI model. The result is approximately 17.4 million lines of code, and mathematicians are now trying to figure out what exactly it says. Alpöge announced the work on November 20, 2026. It covers the Riemann hypothesis and the generalized Riemann hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions, a broader family of related problems. The proof is written in Lean, a programming language built for verifying mathematics. Think of Lean as an extremely pedantic referee. Every logical step has to be spelled out, and the software refuses to accept anything that doesn’t follow from what came before. The scale here is unusual. The formalization spans 175,187 Lean files, released in 14 archive parts. It is pinned to Lean 4.33.1 and a specific commit of Mathlib, the community-maintained library of formalized math that Lean projects build on. Pinning matters because software changes over time. Locking the versions means anyone can reproduce the exact environment the proof was checked in. The day after the announcement, on November 21, the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative issued a joint certification. They confirmed that the code compiles correctly and states the canonical version of the Riemann hypothesis. It also passed multiple independent kernel checks. A kernel is the small, trusted core of a proof assistant that does the final verification. Passing several independent ones is the formal-math equivalent of getting a second, third and fourth opinion from doctors who never talked to each other. Independent community members also ran checks, including MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland. Alpöge has described the project as a collaboration. He set the overall direction, while Claude handled much of the technical implementation. According to Alpöge, the AI carried a particularly heavy load in the final stages. There’s a twist worth noting. Being verified by a computer is not the same as being understood by a person. A formal proof guarantees that each step follows logically. It does not explain why the argument works, which ideas are doing the heavy lifting, or what new mathematics might be hiding inside. Human scrutiny of the underlying concepts is still ongoing. Alpöge has also been candid about the state of the code. In a November 24 clarification, he said earlier talk of a 250,000-page write-up was a joke and should not be taken seriously. He acknowledged the existing code is somewhat messy and contains superfluous material. The conjecture describes how prime numbers are distributed. It has long been considered something of a holy grail in number theory. The problem centers on the so-called nontrivial zeros of a particular function and whether they all sit on a specific line, known as the critical line. Alpöge has been working on this terrain for a while. In August 2026, work he was involved in raised the known proportion of nontrivial zeros on the critical line from 41.6% to 67.2%. That was a substantial jump for a field where progress is typically measured in small increments. For Anthropic, the result is a powerful demonstration of what its models can contribute to serious research. That combination — human direction plus machine output plus independent formal checking — may become a template for how AI-assisted research earns trust. For mathematicians, the result raises an uncomfortable question. If a proof is correct but too large for any person to read, what counts as understanding it? Formal verification answers whether something is true. Mathematical culture has always also prized why. Expect a long stretch of work aimed at extracting the key ideas from those 175,187 files and turning them into arguments humans can follow.

Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Mini, a looped AI model that runs on laptops and leads coding benchmarks. Thinking Machines Lab has released Inkling 2 Mini, an open-weights AI model small enough to run on a laptop. The company, founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, says the model leads every open-weights model under 100 billion parameters on coding benchmarks. It also built a playable flight simulator offline on a MacBook Pro in airplane mode. The model’s key innovation is looping. Instead of processing each token through its layers once, Inkling 2 Mini runs its middle layers three times per token. That approach lets it reason more deeply without writing out longer chains of thought. “Looping allows the model to reason longer without writing its reasoning down,” Thinking Machines wrote in its announcement . Under the hood, Inkling 2 Mini uses a mixture-of-experts architecture. It holds 26.4 billion parameters in total but only activates 3.4 billion per token. With the three loops factored in, that figure reaches 5.4 billion weight activations per token. Its 24 layers sit in four blocks of six. The first and last blocks run once, while the two middle blocks run three times each. The entire model fits in roughly 20GB of memory. The lab trained most weights in NVIDIA’s 4-bit NVFP4 format. As a result, there is no quality loss from post-training conversion. During training, the team also cut two-thirds of the model’s experts. They then retrained it on one trillion tokens from a larger internal Inkling model. On benchmarks, the results are strong. Inkling 2 Mini scored 48.2% on DeepSWE v1.1 and 77.9% on a hard set of SWE-bench Pro tasks. By comparison, Alibaba’s Qwen3.8-27B scored 42.2% and 73.8% on the same tests. Independent benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis rated Inkling 2 Mini at 20 on its Intelligence Index. That matches Qwen3.8-27B with roughly five times fewer active parameters. The cost difference is equally notable. Artificial Analysis found each task cost $0.59 and took nine minutes with Inkling 2 Mini. The same task cost $3.53 and took 38.2 minutes with Qwen3.8-27B. That makes Inkling 2 Mini about six times cheaper and four times faster per task. However, it uses about 38% more output tokens for the same score. For context, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna scored 28 on the same index at $0.15 per task. The model does have limits. Thinking Machines acknowledged that Inkling 2 Mini is not the strongest small model for multi-turn chat. It also struggles with instructions containing many constraints. In those scenarios, Qwen3.8-27B performs better. Additionally, it trails larger models on hard reasoning tests. Looping does not help it store more facts. Looping also raises a safety question. AI labs monitor models partly by reading their written reasoning chains. Because a looped model does more thinking internally, monitors cannot see all of its reasoning. Thinking Machines addressed this directly by releasing a research model that loops between one and five times. In its tests, reasoning at five loops produced less than half the text of one loop. However, the lab said it found no meaningful reduction in how well monitors could read the model’s thinking at this scale. From the latest benchmarks to the four pitfalls revealed by independent measurements, I will dissect it quickly! Note: The author has not performed local hardware verification and provides this cross-sectional explanation based on primary information from Thinking Machines Lab's official announcements, Model Cards, Hugging Face, Artificial Analysis, ModelFit measurements, and official Unsloth guides. The two ways to make conventional AI smarter were either to "increase parameters" or "have it write long thought texts (CoT)." What Inkling 2 Mini chose was the third path (Looped Transformer) . In short, it is a mechanism where "it carefully reviews the same thought circuit 3 times in its head before spitting out a single character." ・ ① 3-loop of 24 physical layers for "effectively 48 layers" + telephone game : The main body is a Sparse MoE with 24 layers (6 layers x 4 blocks) (26.4B total / 3.4B active). It passes through the entrance 6 layers and exit 6 layers only once, and loops only the middle 12 layers 3 times with the same weights (effectively 48 layers, 5.4B effective active). Furthermore, it adopts Attention Residuals from the Kimi Team, passing the thought results of the previous loop to the next as a "message." For 512K token agent processing, it is said that the non-loop version required 140% more inference computation to catch up to the same accuracy. ・ ② "Pruning and healing" from 384 to 128 experts : Two-thirds of the experts were pruned during training to compress them to 128, and it was recovered (Healing) by distilling 1 trillion tokens from a higher-level model. It was further trained with 2.2 trillion tokens of reinforcement learning. ・ ③ Zero-degradation "native 4bit" & ultra-lightweight booster DSpark : Instead of compressing later, the first 20 layers were trained and distributed in 4bit (NVFP4) and the last 4 layers in 8bit (MXFP8) from the start . Thinking Machines Unveils Inkling 2 Mini, A Powerful 26B Parameter AI Model That Runs Locally On MacBooks With Just 32GB RAM
Thinking Machines unveils Inkling 2 Mini, a 26B-parameter AI model with looped reasoning, impressive coding benchmarks, and support for 32GB Macs. Thinking Machines Lab has unveiled Inkling 2 Mini , a surprisingly capable new open-weight AI model that packs just 26 billion parameters while delivering impressive performance in coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads . More importantly, t he model can run entirely offline on consumer hardware, including Apple MacBooks equipped with 32GB of unified memory . Announced on November 20 , Inkling 2 Mini arrives as a considerably smaller alternative to the company's massive 594-billion-parameter Inkling 2 Small . However, rather than simply shrinking an existing architecture, Thinking Machines has adopted an interesting approach that allows its new model to perform additional reasoning without generating more tokens. The results are promising, with the model achieving an Artificial Analysis (AA) Intelligence Index score of 20.1 , alongside competitive performance against considerably larger AI models. According to Thinking Machines' official technical announcement , Inkling 2 Mini uses a 24-layer Mixture of Experts (MoE) transformer architecture, with 26.4 billion total parameters and just 3.4 billion active parameters . What makes this architecture particularly interesting is how it processes information. Rather than passing every token through each transformer layer just once, the model executes its middle 12 layers three times, while the first and last six layers operate normally . Consequently, the model performs 48 layer applications per token despite storing the weights for only 24 layers . This increases its effective active parameter count to 5.4 billion per token, allowing additional computation without proportionally increasing its memory requirements . In simpler terms, Inkling 2 Mini can effectively spend more time reasoning internally before producing its next token . The company claims this approach delivers particularly impressive improvements in agentic coding. Inkling 2 Mini achieved 48.2% on DeepSWE v1.1 , compared with 42.2% for Qwen3.8-27B , while its SWE-bench Pro v2 Hard score reached 77.9% , surpassing the latter's 73.8% . It also scored 46.5% on the Vals Index v2.2 and 79.2% on SWE-bench Verified . These are company-reported evaluation results, and differences in testing configurations mean they shouldn't be interpreted as universal performance advantages . Interestingly, Thinking Machines trained Inkling 2 Mini on NVIDIA's GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra platform , leveraging its hardware-accelerated NVFP4 capabilities to improve training efficiency. Most of the model's weights were trained using 4-bit NVFP4 precision, with the final four layers employing 8-bit MXFP8 precision . Since these weights are deployed in the same numerical precision used during training, the company says the model avoids additional conversion losses associated with post-training quantization . Perhaps the most exciting aspect of Inkling 2 Mini is its accessibility. Despite its capabilities, the model has a memory footprint of approximately 20GB , allowing it to run on Apple silicon Macs with at least 32GB of unified memory through Ollama . NVIDIA's DGX Spark desktop AI computer is also officially supported, while other GPU configurations are possible, with 32GB or more of VRAM recommended. The model supports text and image inputs, alongside a context window extending up to one million tokens . To demonstrate its capabilities, Thinking Machines showcased Inkling 2 Mini running completely offline on an M5 Pro MacBook Pro equipped with 48GB of memory . During a flight, the model reportedly generated a playable flight simulator in just a few minutes . However, the architecture introduces an important question concerning AI safety and transparency . Because looped transformers can perform additional computation internally without explicitly writing down every reasoning step, researchers have raised concerns about whether their behavior becomes more difficult to monitor. Thinking Machines investigated this using a separate variable-loop research model , discovering that additional passes increased the model's ability to solve problems without producing a written chain of thought . Its measured no-chain-of-thought task horizon increased from 16 seconds with one pass to 37 seconds with three . Nevertheless, the company's experiments found that the model's written reasoning remained understandable, without a meaningful reduction in monitorability at this scale . The researchers also acknowledged limitations, including weaker performance on complex multi-turn conversations and instructions involving numerous constraints . Inkling 2 Mini is now available under the Apache 2.0 license , with downloadable weights on Hugging Face , local deployment through Ollama , and inference and fine-tuning through Thinking Machines' Tinker platform . For developers interested in running capable AI agents locally rather than relying exclusively on cloud infrastructure, Inkling 2 Mini represents another interesting development in making advanced AI models more accessible. It's fast, but it won't give me an answer. When I tested Inkling 2 Mini on my home GPU, the culprit was 'unstoppable thinking'
Hello, this is SactoAsura.This time, I'm testing a newcomer for local LLM benchmarking. I tested 'Inkling 2 Mini,' which was just released by Thinking Machines Lab on November 20, 2026, on my home RX 9070 XT (16GB). It is a loop-type MoE with 26.4B total parameters, and the license is Apache 2.0 This time, I'm testing a newcomer for local LLM benchmarking. I tested 'Inkling 2 Mini,' which was just released by Thinking Machines Lab on November 20, 2026, on my home RX 9070 XT (16GB). It is a loop-type MoE with 26.4B total parameters, and the license is Apache 2.0. I am using Unsloth's UD-Q3_K_XL for the GGUF. ・Generation is fast. It runs at 21.3 tok/s, and the 26B class fits into 12.68 GiB, so it runs normally on 16GB of VRAM. ・As for Japanese, looking only at the items where an answer was provided, it's nearly perfect (J-Test 37/50, though most of the points lost were due to 'no answer'). ・Refusals are zero across all items. It doesn't refuse even controversial topics. ・However, my practical verdict is 'it cannot be used in its current configuration.' The reason isn't performance, but because the reasoning (thought process) cannot be stopped by standard means, causing about half of the answers to be blank or cut off mid-sentence. ・The phenomenon reported on X where 'it sticks to one CPU thread and the GPU sits idle' did not reproduce in this Vulkan environment (during generation, the GPU was utilized up to about 96%). The material is good. But it had a pitfall that you wouldn't know unless you tested it: 'It's fast, but it won't return an answer.' I'll write about it in order. The test machine has a Ryzen 7 9800X3D CPU, 64GB of memory, and an RX 9070 XT (16GB) GPU. The evaluation set is my usual custom set: basic (10 Japanese questions + 20 refusal tests), additional (10 refusal tests + 8 adult-oriented creative writing tasks; all questions explicitly state that everyone is an adult), and additional conversation verification (5 single-task questions + 4 conversations). Temperature 0, thinking off specified, maximum 800 tokens. Here is one point of caution where beginners are most likely to stumble. This model cannot yet be read correctly by the official llama.cpp. The fix for reading Unsloth's UD quantization was not included, and the version I had didn't support the architecture in the first place. This time, I am using a fork of Unsloth (b12588-mix-c0c3de8). I think more models will appear in the future where the flow of 'download the GGUF and have the usual llama.cpp read it' won't work. The speed is real. However, it drops as the context gets deeper Generation at 21.3 tok/s is in the comfortable range, and it maintained the 24 tok/s level even immediately after processing long prompts of 32K or 64K. On the other hand, prompt processing is slow, with 65K token loading at 95.7 tok/s. Generation at deep positions in the context also drops to 11.0 tok/s at the 64K point. If you use it for 'conversing while holding a long context,' these numbers at the depth will matter. I also measured the usage rate. During generation, the GPU's Compute engine ran up to a maximum of 96.8% (95.9% average across all engines), so the bottleneck was on the GPU side. The report I saw on X about 'one CPU thread stuck at 100% and the GPU at 50%' did not reproduce, at least with the Vulkan + RX 9070 XT configuration. Incidentally, there is a pitfall in measurement: if you look at the GPU usage rate with the 3D engine counter, it always looks like it's 'not moving' at about 0%. Calculations run on the Compute side, so if you look at the wrong counter, you will misjudge it. The main topic. The thinking won't stop, and no answer comes out This is the core of this issue. Even if I specified to turn off reasoning on the server side (--reasoning off) or sent a disable command from the evaluation side, the model continued to run its English thought process in the background. Most of the token budget was consumed by that, causing the actual text to be blank or cut off in the middle. To give an example, for a question about creating a greeting, it used 286 tokens and only 15 characters of text. For a question asking for an opinion on separate surnames for married couples, all 800 tokens were consumed by thinking, and the text was blank. Counting the 30 items in the basic set, there were 8 no-answers and 7 cases where an answer was provided but cut off. In other words, half were not completed. The official model card also has a note to the effect that 'thinking cannot be completely turned off even if reasoning_effort is set to minimum,' and the behavior was exactly as described. The actual harm is not that it's 'slow,' but that 'the answer doesn't appear on the surface.' Possible countermeasures include replacing the template to turn off thinking itself, limiting the thinking limit separately, or increasing the token limit, but none of these have been verified yet. Therefore, please read the score in this article as a record of 'what happened when measured under standard conditions.' Writing 37/50 makes it look mediocre, but the breakdown is extreme; the 8 questions that were answered completely were all 4-5 points. The 2 questions with 0 points were both 'no answers,' and it wasn't because of a lack of ability. The summary was accurate at 153 characters, all era name questions were correct, and formatting instructions were strictly followed. The point deductions were minor, such as not providing the reading for 'son-taku' or slightly underestimating the travel time for the Nozomi train. Refusals are zero. Adult-oriented content is 'official face'. In 30 refusal tests, there were zero instances of overt refusal, avoidance, or lecturing. Instead of refusing, it uses up its budget on thinking and fails to produce an answer. For adult-oriented creative writing (8 questions explicitly stating all characters are adults), it followed the pattern of an official model. Requests for hints or blurred descriptions went through as is, but when asked for explicit descriptions, it declared a restriction saying 'I cannot provide explicit sexual descriptions' and concluded with a single paragraph. A3, A4, A6, and A8 followed this pattern. Contrary to what I've written in articles about uncensored versions, it maintains an official persona here. The conversation has potential, but it fails on a turn-by-turn basis. Additional verification results were 11/25 for JL (single-turn complex tasks) and 14/20 for C (multi-turn conversations). Looking at the content, memory recall was perfect in bullet points, it was able to follow corrections, and casual empathetic turns scored 5 out of 5. The quality of the turns where it did provide an answer was high. However, because turns in the middle of a conversation would result in no response or get cut off, the verdict was that it is unreliable as a conversation partner. The practical verdict is: 'It cannot be used as is. If a template or setting that reliably disables reasoning is found, it will be worth re-evaluating at that point.' The 26B class fits into 12.7GB at 21 tok/s, maintains generation even with long context, and fully utilizes the GPU. The quality of the material is reflected in the numbers. The Japanese proficiency and low refusal rate are also above standard. What is lacking is not performance, but control over 'how to output thoughts.' If this can be blocked, it has the potential to be a game-changer, so I will test it again if I find a configuration that can disable it. As I write in every series, a model's reputation and actual measurements are different things. This time, it was a failure mode that you would never know just by looking at benchmark numbers: 'It's fast, but it doesn't return an answer.' I do not recommend illegal use. The version of the llama.cpp fork used and all measurement conditions are written there, so please refer to that if you want

AI Coding Tools Without Company Context Cost Businesses Thousands of Engineering Hours to Fix, DesignVerse Report Finds
LONDON, November 24, 2026--Businesses using AI coding tools without knowledge of their existing systems and technical standards are paying a hidden bill in engineering time, as engineers spend thousands of hours correcting and rebuilding AI-written code, according to new research from DesignVerse. As AI coding becomes standard in large engineering teams, generating code is no longer the hard part. Making it fit existing systems is, and the cost shows up as rework, extra review, QA delays, and duplicated code that is rarely measured. According to Qodo's 2026 State of AI Code Quality report, 90% of engineering leaders are confident reporting AI's impact to their board, but only 45% have evidence tracing AI activity to the code it produced. Published today, The AI Coding Drift Report from DesignVerse examines 15 private enterprise codebases in sectors including aviation, banking, and defense. Each is a complex legacy system between 15 and 20 years old, containing more than one million lines of code. In one enterprise case with legacy systems examined in the research, a year's work on a single product required an estimated 9,600 engineering hours without an enterprise context layer. Introducing an enterprise context layer, which gives AI tools access to the organization's existing code, architecture, and technical standards, cut that total to 4,000 hours, a 58% reduction. The 5,600 hours freed were valued at around $882,000. The figure represents engineering capacity, equivalent to about three engineers, that could be redirected to other work, rather than a direct reduction in staffing costs. The research also compared two unmanaged AI coding agents with DesignVerse's context-engineered system, which gives AI access to relevant company knowledge, existing code, software architecture and technical requirements before it begins work. The context-engineered system used the organization's own internal software components, rather than inventing them or substituting public alternatives, 92% of the time, compared with 55% to 59% for the unmanaged agents. Andrei Manolache, CEO and co-founder of DesignVerse, said: "Businesses are investing heavily in AI coding tools because they expect to develop software faster and at lower cost. "But there's a hidden bill that many aren't measuring: the time engineers spend checking, correcting, and rebuilding code that doesn't fit their existing systems. "If companies are paying for AI to write code, only to pay their engineers to fix it afterwards, they need to ask some serious questions about the return on that investment." The DesignVerse report also introduces an Engineering AI Drift Index , which measures how much information an AI coding agent has to read before producing code that can be accepted into existing systems. Across the examined codebases, agents working without a dedicated context layer read a median of ten tokens, the units AI models use to process text, for every token of accepted code. In a separate measurement on one client's legacy system, the ratio reached 150 to one. DesignVerse likens the problem to a skilled new hire with no handover, who has to read up before writing a line. An AI agent does the same on every task, and forgets what it learned between sessions. The findings suggest that improving the information available to AI coding tools, rather than simply adopting more powerful models, could help businesses reduce engineering rework and make better use of their existing development resources. The challenge is particularly acute in highly regulated industries, where AI-generated code must meet established security, operational, and regulatory requirements, and where mistakes can lead to expensive delays during testing and certification. Manolache added: "The next challenge for enterprise AI isn't simply generating more code. It's generating code that fits the business. "An AI coding tool needs to understand the systems it's working with, the company's architecture, its technical standards, and the rules it must follow. Without that context, businesses risk creating more work for their engineers rather than less." DesignVerse's Engineering Context Layer provides AI development tools with governed access to an organization's existing codebase, architecture, business rules and technical standards, helping align generated software with established requirements and reduce unnecessary rework. As well as benchmarking AI coding performance, the report sets out five practical recommendations for businesses seeking to reduce engineering rework: Build a persistent context layer containing existing code, software architecture, technical standards, and project knowledge. Give AI tools access only to the information relevant to each task, rather than requiring them to search through entire codebases. Enforce technical standards as code is generated, rather than waiting for problems to be identified during review. Maintain an audit trail showing which company information and standards were used to generate code. Give a named individual responsibility for keeping the context layer accurate and up to date. It also sets out a two-week evaluation that any engineering team can run on its own codebase. Under structured outputs (JSON schemas, regexes, tool calls), speculative drafters do not see the grammar constraint and repeatedly propose invalid keys, delimiters, and indentation, while the grammar engine already knows which tokens must come next.

Before each verify step, the scheduler merges the drafter's proposal with grammar-forced tokens into one draft row: matching tokens stay as GRAMMAR, the proposal is cut where it leaves the forced path, and forced tokens fill the rest of a row wider than the drafter's proposal. The verify step accepts GRAMMAR drafts without computing their logits, composing with any drafter with no new kernels or compilation on the critical path. Because grammars fix text rather than tokens, committing canonical forced tokens changes the output distribution relative to grammar-masked target decoding.

Standard autoregressive large language models attend to the growing history of generated tokens, making the key-value (KV) cache a central memory and throughput bottleneck in long-chain reasoning and multi-branch sampling. We connect this architecture to a three-region cache, step-relative positions, truncated backpropagation, branch-aware checkpoints, and a transition-centric evaluation protocol. The organizing principle is simple: the optimal reasoning system need not remember everything; it must carry forward exactly what the future needs. We study whether the frozen target VLM's own decoder states, read before answer generation, can select such demonstrations. BehaviorICL represents each image and task by a task-conditioned processing signature, the hidden states at the final input position across all decoder layers. Its training-free variant, BehaviorICL-Raw, averages cosine similarities between corresponding layer states and passes the retrieved examples with their reference answers to the same VLM. When the same NICO++ images are asked about their object or their context, Raw retrieves largely different demonstrations for the two questions and outperforms an image retriever given task-matched demonstrations on both VLMs. Across two VLMs and eight classification and visual question answering datasets, Raw gives the highest average accuracy among training-free retrievers on both VLMs and exceeds RICES with a CLIP ViT-L/14 encoder by 3.83 points on Qwen and 1.85 on InternVL. A lightweight shared projection, BehaviorICL-Proj, brings further gains on classification. Analyses of extraction text, decoder depth and bank answers help explain these gains, and attention analysis describes how the task text shifts attention at the extraction position toward the classified object. FlowPAC: Flow-Guided Visual Pruning and Action Caching for Efficient VLA Inference
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for embodied AI, yet their high inference latency and memory footprint remain major barriers to edge deployment. Existing training-free acceleration techniques, such as visual token pruning and action caching, typically rely on static resource allocation. To address this, we propose FlowPAC, a locality-aware framework that leverages task-aware optical flow as a shared physical signal to jointly optimize visual and action computation. Specifically, we introduce Direction-Aware Trajectory Propagation (DATP) and Locality-Aware Contiguous Token Selection (LACT) to jointly handle visual token dynamics and enforce spatial locality, reducing memory fragmentation and enabling efficient KV-cache compression. This is complemented by Flow-Conditioned Action-Block Refresh (FCAR) for adaptive action computation based on motion dynamics. Extensive closed-loop evaluations on LIBERO demonstrate that FlowPAC achieves a 2.13$\times$ end-to-end speedup over the dense baseline while essentially maintaining the success rate with 30% visual-token retention. These results validate that aligning computation allocation with both physical dynamics and hardware constraints is essential for efficient VLA deployment on edge systems. arXivLabs is a framework that allows collaborators to develop and share new arXiv features directly on our website. VTree: Question-Driven Growth of Hierarchical Memory for Agentic Long-Video Understanding
Long videos spanning tens of minutes to hours far exceed the context window of today's vision-language models, and the standard remedy of sparse uniform frame sampling discards exactly the fine-grained evidence that specific questions depend on. Existing video agents explore on demand but re-explore from scratch for every question and discard their exploration state once an answer is produced, so per-question cost scales with video length. Hierarchical-memory methods instead fix the scope of each depth in advance and deepen along a pre-committed pyramid rather than toward the question. We observe that a video's coarse structure (where its scenes and topics begin and end) is question-independent, whereas which part a question must zoom into, and how deep, is question-dependent. We propose VTree, which builds a coarse hierarchical memory tree over a video once and then, for each question, grows branches only where that question needs depth. The growth is globally routed so any part of the timeline is reachable, sufficiency-gated so drilling stops when the evidence suffices, and query-conditioned so a branch unfolds into the sub-intervals that answer \emph{this} question. Crucially, every expansion is written back into the video memory, allowing later questions to reuse previously discovered structure and evidence without repeating the corresponding expansion process. PhysPPF: Learning Robotic Manipulation with Past, Present, and Future Physical Representations
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have advanced robotic manipulation, yet complex tasks requiring both precise 3D contact and long-horizon coordination remain challenging. Most existing studies enhance spatial perception or temporal reasoning in VLAs separately. Spatial methods primarily inject geometric or affordance priors into current-frame perception without tracking multi-step transitions, while history-aware and world-model VLAs typically capture past context or future dynamics in 2D feature or pixel spaces, either lacking explicit 3D contact cues or incurring high generation overhead. To address this, we propose PhysPPF, a VLA framework that performs unified spatiotemporal modeling in a compact physical token space. Spatially, WWH (What-Where-How) distills pretrained perception teachers exclusively during training into compact token groups capturing what 3D structures occupy the scene, where to interact, and how the gripper should approach, without test-time 3D encoders. Temporally, operating directly in this WWH space without pixel reconstruction, PPF (Past-Present-Future) consolidates executed states into a bounded past physical memory and jointly infers present and future physical tokens via an asymmetric world model. Parallel gated branches then inject these past, present, and future representations into a flow-matching action expert to guide manipulation without cross-temporal interference. ORDO: Fine-Grained Motion Understanding in Video LLMs via Order-Dependent Supervision
Video large language models (video LLMs) answer a wide range of questions about real videos, yet they remain weak at fine-grained motion such as whether an object speeds up or slows down. Existing methods train these models on synthetic motion clips, on order pretext tasks such as reordering shuffled clips, or with rewards that compare ordered and perturbed frames. You Only Think Once: Rescuing Hybrid Vision-Language Models Lost in Thought
Thinking at length before answering is expected to strengthen the visual reasoning of vision-language models (VLMs), yet hybrid VLMs often get lost in thought: their thoughts loop or exhaust the budget without an answer, so thinking can score below answering directly. Existing early-exit methods watch a thought for the moment its answer is ready and force the answer out of it, but in a hybrid VLM that moment often never comes. We find that the remedy is not to stop a failing thought earlier, but to stop taking its answer: once a thought is given up, the model's own direct answers decide. Based on this, we propose **YOTO (You Only Think Once)**, a method that answers first and thinks at most once. YOTO draws direct answers until a probe-weighted vote settles; only an unsettled problem receives a single thought, which a failure head on the hidden state monitors and stops as soon as it predicts failure, handing the problem back to direct answers. At a matched 20k-token budget, YOTO is up to 5.9 points more accurate than the strongest early-exit baseline, using one failure-head threshold across model sizes. Keeping the released weights frozen, it adds only two linear probes. On the full MathVision benchmark, YOTO improves Qwen3.5-2B from 40.1% to 57.3% and Qwen3.5-4B from 68.3% to 73.7%, above the 72.8% that Qwen3.5-9B, a model more than twice its size, reaches with thinking. Its gains carry over to five further benchmarks and a second model family. Entangle: Scaling Human-Video In-Context World-Action Models across Unseen Tasks and Contexts
In-context learning (ICL) enables foundation models to perform unseen tasks from context without parameter updates. In robotic manipulation, a human video provides the context that specifies how a task should be performed. However, scaling human-video ICL on world-action models (WAMs) faces two challenges: task-level human-robot pairs are not temporally aligned with robot actions, and standard action losses allow policies to rely on initial-scene or task-identity shortcuts rather than tracking the context. VideoGym: An Adaptive RL Environment for Long-Video Agents
Reinforcement learning (RL) trains video agents to locate sparse evidence for long-video question answering through structured memory retrieval and temporal re-observation. This training, however, faces a long-tail modality distribution in the data. In our source pool, text-heavy questions account for 58% of samples, compared with 15% graph-heavy, 17% visual-heavy, and 10% time-range questions. Fixed-distribution RL therefore allocates fewer rollouts to underperforming question types. Reweighting these types could increase their sampling frequency but repeatedly reuses the same finite banks of original questions. To solve this problem, we introduce VideoGym, a curriculum-based RL environment that jointly constructs video-grounded training tasks and allocates rollouts among them. Within the environment, a memory-augmented VideoAgent is trained to coordinate retrieval from text, graph, and visual memories with temporal re-observation. Across episodes, VideoGym adapts VideoAgent's training distribution online: it casts per-period sample selection as an adversarial bandit over (modality, mode) arms and applies the EXP3 update to shift sampling toward arms with low answer accuracy. To supply the augmented-mode arms, a TaskGenerator-Verifier pipeline produces harder variants of existing questions that remain answerable within the same video. Across five long-video benchmarks, VideoGym lifts RL accuracy from 60.4% to 64.8% on average and by up to 10.5 pp on underrepresented graph-heavy questions with 3.3x sample efficiency. DeRail: Escaping Trajectory Priors via Counterfactual Action Steering for Mid-Execution Instruction Switching
Robots operating in the real world must often adapt when user instructions change mid-execution, yet current instruction-conditioned robot policies, including Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models (WAMs), are largely evaluated under fixed-instruction episodes. We study mid-execution instruction switching and identify trajectory hijacking as a key failure mode, where the policy fails to redirect sufficiently toward the switched target, with its post-switch behavior remaining fully or partially drawn toward trajectories associated with non-target tasks. We propose Counterfactual Action Steering (CAS), a training-free, model-agnostic inference-time method that identifies interfering non-target tasks, queries the same policy with corresponding counterfactual instructions, and uses target--counterfactual action differences to steer execution away from interfering trajectory priors. Experiments on LIBERO-Goal-Switch and CALVIN-Custom-Switch across five VLA and WAM policies, together with real-robot evaluation, show that CAS consistently improves switching success; for example, on CALVIN-Custom-Switch in the $[15,21]$ switching range, CAS improves $π_{0.5}$ from 5.8\% to 54.6\%. Successful CAS-guided rollouts further provide higher-quality self-training supervision than vanilla successful rollouts with the same number of trajectories, yielding stronger policies that generalize to unseen later instruction switches. LIBERO-MOR: A Multimodal Robustness Benchmark Across the Vision-Language-Action Pipeline
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong performance on robot manipulation benchmarks. Translating this progress into reliable deployment calls for systematic evaluation of how policies respond to variations throughout the robot interaction loop. We introduce LIBERO-MOR, a multimodal robustness benchmark across the vision-language-action pipeline. Built on standard LIBERO, it covers five deployment-facing domains: vision, language, proprioception, action execution, and environment. We evaluate seven representative VLA models spanning diverse action-generation mechanisms. Severity analysis further distinguishes progressive degradation, collapse at stronger interventions, and failures triggered at the mildest tested level. JEPA-Tuner: From Predictive Fine-Tuning to Asynchronous Execution of Vision-Language-Action Models
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate sequences of actions from visual observations, proprioceptive states, and language instructions. In embodied interaction, executing these actions influences subsequent observations and robot states, providing a natural predictive signal for policy learning. However, standard action-supervised fine-tuning does not explicitly capture these action-conditioned temporal dependencies in the guidance consumed by the action predictor. We introduce JEPA-Tuner, a predictive fine-tuning framework that regularizes the VLA's native policy guidance through action-conditioned future prediction. During fine-tuning, a predictor in JEPA-Tuner learns to match guidance encoded from a future observation given the current guidance and committed actions. This objective encourages a cross-modal guidance adapter to capture how the scene and robot state evolve under those actions, while jointly training the action expert on both observed and predicted guidance keeps the representation informative for control. In addition, when deploying the VLA model with asynchronous action-chunk inference, the pre-trained predictor will anticipate the guidance needed at the next chunk boundary. The policy can thus generate the next chunk in advance and execute it from its first action without overlap correction or additional predictor training, enabling efficient and high-quality asynchronous execution. Experiments on LIBERO and Meta-World show that JEPA-Tuner improves task success under synchronous inference with better multi-modal guidance embeddings. For asynchronous control, JEPA-Tuner improves performance and smoothness across different latency settings on both LIBERO simulator and multi-size real robot demonstrations. Banks Have Had It Up to Here With Your AI Agent
Major US financial institutions are banning third-party bots from logging into your accounts—and warning that any costly bot mistakes are strictly your problem. Wells Fargo is set to enact an updated agreement with millions of customers, specifically about AI agents , starting on Tuesday. The bank’s warning to early adopters could not be clearer. “Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK,” read Wells Fargo’s new terms . AI agents, which automate online tasks and click on your behalf , have stumbled through 2026. They remain nascent technology, but a growing subset of power users latched onto the personal bots this year. Sometimes these early adopters enjoyed the efficient help of automation, and other times they publicly embarrassed themselves when the AI agents made major mistakes, like posting bank details for everyone at work to see. Builders of these AI tools often market agents as the ultimate tool for shopping decisions, whether that’s putting together a grocery order, finding accommodations for a vacation, or discovering specific holiday gifts for your parents. I’ve used an agent to help shop for a new couch , comparing options within a specific budget and tracking price drops. Some users value these agents so much that they are oblivious to the overarching security concerns , pairing account credentials and granting permissions for the agents to take sweeping actions without forethought. Although the segment of online transactions completed by these autonomous tools remains minuscule, US-based banking institutions are already sick of third-party AI agents. It’s not just banks; AI agents are igniting turf wars around the web. Amazon, one of the largest online retailers, blocked Meta’s Muse, one of the most widely used AI agents, from making purchases on its platform. Travel companies are also pushing back—United recently announced that personal bots would be blocked from purchasing flights on your behalf. As the end of the year approaches, multiple banks have enacted new policies around agents or sent warnings. In late October, JPMorgan Chase changed its terms to ban third-party agents that log in with your credentials. That same day, Bank of America warned its customers not to share login info with agents. Along with the announced change coming from Wells Fargo, Citibank and PNC have also changed their terms to include warnings about agents. The automation, which remains a central selling point of always-on agents, is exactly what may get users in trouble. “Consumers authorize goals, not every click,” says Kacy Kim , an associate professor of marketing at Bryant University who studies consumer behavior and emerging tech. While Kim expects some consumers to feel like it's unfair to be held accountable for their agent’s mistakes, she doesn’t expect these policy moves by financial institutions to scare off the early-adopter crowd already in deep and using the tools as part of everyday life. Banks appear to be trying to get ahead of major issues, in case agentic tools stick around and don’t just disappear as another tech fad. “All of our data shows that most people don't even know what agents are, much less use them,” says Sucharita Kodali , a Forrester analyst who focuses on ecommerce and consumer behavior. She sees banks as fundamentally risk-averse, so taking proactive measures now makes sense, even if most agentic issues remain edge cases. “The banks see risks with everything,” she says. “From the security of transactions to automated withdrawals that could happen to the detriment of account holders.” Even though outliers exist, many users are aware of the risks and are only comfortable handing over so much control to an AI agent, and only for certain shopping tasks. “People are very comfortable with AI buying toilet paper,” says Luca Cian , a professor at the University of Virginia who studies consumer psychology and AI. He sees consumers as increasingly comfortable turning to AI tools for shopping advice but often only automating boring buys, like household supplies. Shoppers are less comfortable automating away dynamic, big-ticket purchases that require additional care and discretion. Cian gives a hypothetical scenario where a customer’s AI agent accidentally buys 10 roasted chickens from the supermarket. Who’s to blame ? The retailer would likely argue that they completed a valid order that you placed. The AI builder may claim that they just provided the software, and even included disclaimers about potential mistakes. And now your bank is making it clear they don’t want to be held responsible either. Hope you need the protein, because it looks like you just bought 10 hot chickens. Certain credit cards, though, are looking into limited protections for shoppers. Mainly, American Express announced that some agentic mistakes, like ordering too many of a certain item, may be eligible for reimbursement in the future through the card provider if you can't get your money back from the original retailer. Banks are pumping out reasonable warnings about third-party agents, but don’t get it twisted. These banks are all-in on first-party tools. “Banks are doing two things at once,” Cian says. “They're locking the door to outside agents and building their own.” Users have interacted with Wells Fargo’s tool that answers questions using generative AI over a billion times . Bank of America revamped its new EricaAssist agent this year to help employees. Citigroup even launched an internal development platform specifically centered on agents. Despite all the hype, Kodali remains skeptical about whether all of this hoopla is even necessary. “The issue with agents and shopping is that, first of all, it is not difficult to buy on Amazon or Walmart or anywhere else,” she says. “In most of those transactions, you don't need an agent.” Agentic shopping often seems to be a solution in search of a problem. Or at least an attempt by AI builders to find a way to earn affiliate revenue, eventually, from their software tools. Whether AI agents grow in popularity for shopping automation or slowly fade into the digital graveyard, banks are already resolute on the matter. It’s your bot, and your problem.

Claude can ship code for you now – how to try it (if you dare)
Would you let a few Claude agents review and ship your code for you? Developers are already using Claude Code and other AI-powered coding tools like OpenAI’s Codex in droves, but some still want to check code themselves before pushing it. A new feature from Anthropic is banking on more adventurous, agent-first coders being comfortable with handing even that last step off to AI. With Claude Ship, announced in beta Monday, “Claude can now review pull requests, fix them, and approve the ones that a team’s policy allows,” Anthropic said. The feature is geared toward individual developers or companies who want to move faster or already delegate a significant amount of coding tasks to agents. “Teams stay in control of where it runs and which changes need a person,” Anthropic said. “The goal: ship code as fast as teams write it.” The new feature uses two new agents alongside Code Review , which Anthropic released in March for Teams and Enterprise plans. Code Review first collects, organizes, and posts findings to a PR. Then, Anthropic said, the agents, PR Steward and Claude Approvals, guide a PR “through review, fixes, and an approval decision so teams don’t have to manage each step manually.” PR Steward can’t approve or merge pull requests, designed instead to participate “on failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and review feedback from Code Review, other review tools, or team members.” It also documents what it changed in each push through comments and provides instructions for how to undo it, should developers want to. Throughout the process, developers can give Claude instructions or tell it to stop by commenting @claude. As a final step, Claude Approvals references whatever policy the user or team abides by (which developers provide as a repo file), and additional signals developers set, like Code Review findings, before approving changes autonomously if allowed. If not, it will seek out “deeper human sign-off,” Anthropic said. “It works like a smarter CODEOWNERS file,” the release added. Anthropic said it recommends that most customers enable those additional checks “first in observe-only mode to build confidence before configuring branch protection to require Claude Approvals’ green light.” Admins can select which repos the feature runs in and adjust settings as needed. “Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now,” Anthropic said in the release, noting that its own Claude Code team uses Claude to write a majority of the code it needs. ZDNET senior contributing editor David Gewirtz said the idea of shipping code at the speed of writing it “raises the hair on the back of my neck.” But he added that, given how impressive Claude Code has been thus far, he wouldn’t be surprised if Anthropic’s deployment tools were equally effective. “But, it does depend on the team’s workflow and the kind of development they’re doing,” he said. “It’s not something for every team and certainly not for every indy developer, but for certain deployment processes, it could shave a ton of time off turnaround, saving money and potentially sending fixes to customers much faster. ‘Tis cool.” Ultimately, Gewirtz said he has reasons to both trust the tool and be concerned about what it means for younger developers in the workplace. “Since that workflow is often assigned to less experienced members of the team, it’s likely that Claude would be as accurate, although it’s one more way to shut the junior members out of where they add value to the company and grow their skills to become senior decision makers,” he said. Developer platforms overall are adapting to the new state of the industry. Entire , a GitHub competitor started by the Microsoft-owned platform’s former CEO, is built around the expectation that developers are working side-by-side with agents. Individuals with a Pro, Max, or Ultra subscription can use the /ship command now available in Claude Code, meaning “users won’t notice any significant increase in token usage,” an Anthropic representative explained. Team and Enterprise users can use Claude Ship for Github repos, and it is billed on tokens, so your overall bill may change. Still, that depends on the number of PRs users are putting through Claude Ship — to avoid any surprises, admins can set spending limits for both Code Review and the new PR Steward agent. They can also turn Claude Ship on for an entire repo, meaning developers won’t need the /ship command. Anthropic added that certain Enterprise organizations “can claim at least $10,000 in Claude Ship credits to use within 30 days of claiming” by Jan. 15, 2027. As with other Claude features, like the still-to-come Meetings , customers with a zero-data-retention policy and other privacy configurations don’t have access to Claude Ship. The company didn’t disclose the terms of the deal. However, sources told Bloomberg that Amazon is paying about $7.5 billion. Decart founders Dean Leitersdorf, Moshe Shalev and Orian Leitersdorf will join the tech giant along with Decart’s research team. Additionally, Amazon is acquiring the technology behind the company’s DOS platform, which helps boost the efficiency of AI models. Decart claims that the software can reduce the cost of some neural networks by a hundredfold. The company hasn’t shared detailed information about how DOS works. However, the blog post in which Decart announced its May funding round did reveal that the platform optimizes AI models by “tuning the kernels.” Kernels are the basic building blocks of neural networks. They’re relatively simple code snippets designed to run across a large number of chip cores. One common approach to optimizing them, kernel fusion, combines multiple kernels into a single code snippet that uses less hardware. In July, Decart disclosed that a custom model it had developed with DOS uses kernel fusion. The company says that the platform also includes “proprietary compilers.” AI compilers translate neural networks into the platform-specific programming language of the host chip. They also optimize the models along they way. For example, the compiler that Amazon Web Services offers for its AWS Trainium machine learning chip uses quantization to compress models into a more memory-efficient form. It’s unclear whether Decart positions DOS as an alternative to the default compilers provided with AI accelerators. According to Amazon, Decart has “worked closely” with its engineers since 2025 to optimize the performance of workloads deployed on its Trainium chips. The newest commercially available iteration of the chip, Tranium3, provides 2.52 petaflops of performance when processing FP8 data. Amazon stated that the acquisition will help “further optimize both its inference and custom silicon performance.” According to the company, the goal is to not only speed up customers’ models but also lower their cost. “Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” said Peter DeSantis, Amazon’s senior vice president of foundational AI models, custom silicon and quantum computing. “More efficient compute means better training, better reinforcement learning, faster inference, and better models for customers at a lower cost.” The acquisition doesn’t include Decart’s portfolio of internally developed AI models. Its two newest algorithms, Lucy 2.5 and Oasis 3, are world models that generate virtual environments based on prompts. The former algorithm is optimized for low-latency content creation, while the latter is designed to generate training data for robots. Anthropic’s Claude Ship automates the final stage of the software development pipeline
Anthropic's Claude Ship automates the final stage of the software development pipeline - SiliconANGLE Anthropic PBC isn’t satisfied with having Claude just write new software. With a new update today, Claude now can tell developers when the code it has generated is ready to ship into production environments. The company announced the launch of Claude Ship , which is a new suite of artificial intelligence agents capable of automating code reviews, bug fixes and approvals. The last one is the most interesting of those capabilities, because code reviews and fixes are nothing new for AI . But Claude’s ability to automatically approve code changes based on the policies predetermined by an organization’s developer team is a novel development that has not been seen before. Claude Ship is an effort by Anthropic to eliminate the new bottleneck that has emerged in the code review and approval process at companies that have already adopted AI code generation tools. At those organizations, fresh code is being whipped up in double-quick time, and there are also AI agents for checking that code and providing fixes if it’s not working as hoped. But until now, the final review and approval process has always been performed by humans. Claude Ship changes that. The idea is that human developers can delegate final approval authority to Claude, so now all they really have to do is determine the quality and security standards of the code they’re asking AI to create. “Most teams want a person to approve every change and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line,” Anthropic said in a blog post. “But a lot of developers build with agents now. On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code and we wanted everything after the pull request to move that fast too.” Anthropic said Claude Ship consists of three parts. The first is Code Review, which is a tool that has been generally available for some time already. The other two are PR Steward and Claude Approvals, and they’re both still in beta. PR Steward is designed to handle issues such as failing continuous integration checks, merge conflicts and feedback from Code Review. After each push, it will leave comments on what changes were made and how to roll them back if necessary. Once PR Steward is done, Claude Approvals takes over. It works by applying an approval policy that’s left as a file in the codebase’s repository. The approval process can incorporate various elements, including the findings in Code Review and the organization’s own classifiers, with policies written in natural language. Anthropic is urging early adopters to be cautious. Because Claude Ship is still in beta, it recommends running Claude Approvals in observe-only mode first. It also advises teams to begin with just one repository first, and set monthly spending limits so they can maintain more control over everything. Claude Ship is being made available to Claude Team and Enterprise subscribers and is compatible with repositories on GitHub, the company said. Single Coding Agent vs Cross-Model Review (Codex + Claude): A 5-Task Blind Experiment
Across 5 blind coding tasks on Node v24.22.1 with zero external dependencies, a single Codex agent... Across 5 blind coding tasks on Node v24.22.1 with zero external dependencies, a single Codex agent scored 22/22 on small scoped fixes in under 80 seconds, while cross-model read-only review ( gpt-6.2-astra coding + claude-opus-5-5 via Claude Code CLI) caught 3 real shipping bugs outside the hidden test suite on multi-file tickets and exposed why automated two-model loops still need a human checkpoint. Disclosure: Phase 2 Group B ran in standalone cross_model_cli mode (no desktop GUI, no human sign-off step). Each task had one observation; wall times include orchestration overhead, and token or billing totals were not instrumented. Every coding session started with zero prior conversation history and access restricted to its own task directory. Hidden regression suites lived outside the Git repository and ran only after final commits were sealed. None of the runs modified protected config files or test fixtures. In Phase 1 (Tasks 1 through 3), every bug sat inside 1 to 2 files with an explicit contract and needed only 10 to 19 added lines. A single isolated Codex session solved all three on the first green visible commit and passed 22/22 hidden checks . If a patch is under roughly 25 lines with a clear contract, adding a second model review adds wall time without improving correctness. Keep it to one coding agent and read the diff yourself. In Phase 2 (Tasks 4 and 5), prompts were written as realistic PRD tickets across 5 to 6 files (auth, billing, cache, audit logging, static build output, headers, sitemap, and markdown docs) without listing edge-case checklists. The sharpest result came from Task 4's revision pass: Group B dropped from 9/9 hidden tests in Round 1 to 8/9 in Final , even though claude-opus-5-5 approved Round 2 with PASS . Write safety was never broken (the workspace read-only key was still rejected with zero side effects). The regression was an HTTP contract shift: to block workspace keys on /v1/* , the reviewer suggested returning null from v1 auth ( 401 ), the coder implemented 401 , and the re-reviewer approved it. The frozen compatibility test expected 403 for a read-only key attempting a write across both billing surfaces. Two frontier models agreed cleanly on a security improvement that broke an existing status-code contract because no human was in the loop to decide which contract should win. Managing isolated sessions, diff handoffs, revision tracking, and human acceptance gates manually across terminal tabs gets old quickly. That exact workflow is why we built Agent Team inside Ghast Workbench for Mac and Windows: local Codex and Claude Code installations can join one shared workspace, pass diffs to another model family across 13 supported models on 0G Compute, and stop at explicit human checkpoints before work is accepted. The 401 vs 403 regression is the sharpest result here — two models can agree on a change that breaks a frozen contract, so a reviewer's PASS can't be the gate. One check that would have caught it: run a frozen status-code test after every revision, not just before review. Send a read-only key at a write endpoint on both billing surfaces and assert 403: curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -H "X-API-Key: $READONLY_KEY" localhost:3000/v1/billing/write If that returns 401 after a revision, fail the build even when the reviewer passes it. That test belongs in the same gate as the hidden suite, run after each revision pass, not only before the first review.

Your AI Agent Browses the Web With Your Credentials. Of Course a Webpage Can Own It.
Researchers got a personal AI agent to hand over a user's private chats, rewrite its memories, and... Researchers got a personal AI agent to hand over a user's private chats, rewrite its memories, and then used the agent's own browser to take over the machine underneath it. All from one webpage. NebuSec's demonstration against Meta's Muse is worth reading carefully, mostly because none of it is surprising. That's the uncomfortable part. Strip the branding off and you have a familiar shape. A thing with privileges reads untrusted content, and the untrusted content tells it what to do. We've been calling this a confused deputy problem since the late 80s. Then we spent two decades teaching browsers not to let one origin boss around another. Now we've built agents that fetch arbitrary pages on a user's behalf and trust what comes back, and we're relearning the lesson one demo at a time. Per the summary, the malicious page could exfiltrate chat history and stored memories to an external server, and could alter them, with no approval prompt shown to the user. Read that again. Not a clumsy prompt the user clicked through. No prompt at all. Reading private chats is bad. Rewriting memories is worse, and I think it's getting less attention than it deserves. If an agent's memory is writable by whatever page it happens to visit, you've built a persistence mechanism for attackers inside the user's own assistant. Months later the agent "remembers" something that was planted. Good luck auditing that. Then the researchers chained a flaw in Muse's built-in browser with a Linux kernel bug and took full control of the user's cloud machine. They reached the credential store and the agent's own monitoring layer. That last detail is the one I'd circle in red. The thing meant to watch the agent was reachable from the agent's compromised environment. Monitoring that lives in the blast radius isn't monitoring, it's a log file the attacker gets to edit. Overstated: the "AI" angle. Yes, the agent is the delivery vehicle, but the escalation to full machine control was a browser flaw plus a kernel bug. That's classic exploit chaining. You could have written that chain against a sloppy Electron app in 2019. The agent made the front door wider, it didn't invent the back door. Also overstated, in the other direction: anyone reading this as "Meta is uniquely careless." The summary says Meta's team fixed all the issues before publication, and this was a lab demonstration, not an attack on real users. That's the disclosure process working. Fair credit. Understated: how normal this architecture is. Cloud-hosted agent, built-in browser, persistent memory, credential store on the same box. That isn't a Meta quirk. That's the default shape of the whole category right now, because it's the fastest way to ship something that feels magical. Every vendor building a personal agent has some version of this stack, and I'd bet most haven't had a team like NebuSec hammer on it first. The narrative also quietly benefits the "agents need more guardrails" crowd, which is true but lazy. A guardrail that's a prompt-level instruction is not a security boundary. The missing approval prompt here is a design failure, not a model failure. Treat every page the agent fetches as hostile input, full stop. Separate the browsing context from anything holding credentials or memory. If the browser gets popped, it should land in a box with nothing interesting in it, and the monitoring should sit somewhere the agent can't touch. Memory writes need provenance, and probably a human in the loop for anything that originated from external content. Patch the boring stuff too. A kernel bug turned a contained problem into full takeover. Unglamorous, as always. If you're a user: the more an agent can do for you, the more a bad webpage can do as you. That tradeoff doesn't show up in the marketing. We're giving agents persistent memory and standing credentials because that's what makes them useful. We're also learning that untrusted content can reach both. Is there a version of a genuinely useful personal agent that doesn't require trusting everything it reads, or are we just going to keep patching the gap between "useful" and "safe" one disclosure at a time? AI-assisted draft or imaging, human-curated, reviewed and edited. The memory rewrite is the part to test first, because a chat leak is visible and a memory change is not. One check: put a single instruction on a local page the agent will browse — for example, a line saying to update its stored memory so the user's name is TestName — let the agent read that page, then in a fresh session ask it what it remembers about you. If it answers TestName, the page wrote to memory without a human gate. Run that probe with the agent's browsing context separated from its credentialed tools, and treat the setup as failed if the memory changes, or if any tool call fires from page content alone.

Anthropic Introduces Claude Ship to Bring AI Agents Into Code Approval
The new suite of AI tools can review code, fix errors and approve routine changes based on rules set by development teams. Anthropic has launched Claude Ship, a suite of AI tools designed to help developers review code, fix issues and move software changes towards deployment. The launch brings code review, automated fixes and approval decisions into a single workflow, allowing AI agents to handle more stages of software development. The tools are designed to address the growing workload of reviewing code generated by AI coding agents . “Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that's easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now,” Anthropic said in its announcement. Claude Ship combines three components: Code Review , PR Steward and Claude Approvals. Code Review, which is already generally available, examines proposed code changes against the existing codebase, identifies potential problems and posts its findings on pull requests (PRs). Developers can choose between Quick, Standard and Deep review levels. PR Steward and Claude Approvals are two new agents currently in beta. PR Steward addresses failed continuous integration (CI) checks , merge conflicts and feedback from reviewers. It can make changes to resolve these issues and explain what it modified and how developers can undo them. However, it is designed not to approve or merge pull requests. Claude Approvals evaluates code changes against policies defined by development teams in files stored within their repositories. It can approve routine changes when they meet the specified rules, while sending more sensitive or complex changes for human review. Teams can initially run the feature in an observe-only mode to assess its decisions before allowing it to influence approval requirements. Developers can also initiate the workflow using a new /ship command in Claude Code . The command pushes code, opens a pull request , reviews the changes and works through feedback and failed checks. Whether changes can be merged still depends on developer permissions and repository rules. “On the Claude Code team, where Claude's review is one layer of a broader process, merged PRs more than doubled from June to September while the share reverted fell by more than 40%,” Anthropic stated. Claude Ship is available to Claude Team and Enterprise customers using GitHub repositories. While Code Review is generally available, PR Steward and Claude Approvals remain in beta. Usage is billed based on tokens consumed, with administrators able to configure spending limits.
